However, they found that it was already too late: they did not reach them until they found that the wolf had throttled him and given him several bites.

They snatched him away so he escaped death, but he had looked straight into the next world.
The hound said to him:
— What possesses you, oh young goat, to fly so high?

Source.Title: ܐܿܫܹ݁ܢ ܕ ܬܝܚ̰ܣܝ
Paragraphs: ܝܹܫܪܹܟ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܬܝܒܚܝܪܬ ܕ ܬܝܚ̰ܣܝ. ܐܼܥܘܗܹܕ‑ܝܬ݁ ܣ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ ܐܿܪ ܬ݁‑ܝܹܫ̰݁܃ ܐܿܪ ܝܹܫ̰݁ܝ ܠܹܚܩ‑ܝܣ. ܪܛ̰ܐܢ܃ ܐܿܠܣܹܢ܃ ܙܹܪܥܹܢ ܠ݁ܘܒܝܐܢ. ܘܬܹܢ ܘܐܡܐܢ܃ ܬܹܡܥ̰ܝ܃ ܬܹܙܹ݁ܓܙܹܘ ܐܲܡ ܠܹܒܚܹܪ.
ܝܹܘܹ݁ܨ̰‑ܕ ܐܿܢܹܒܕܘ܃ ܬܹܒܕܐ ܠܐ ܬܹܬ݁ܝܘܪܝܥ̰: ܒܹܓܣܹܢ ܐܲܕ ܬ݁‑ܣ݁ܘܹܢ܄ ܠܐܡܹܥܢܐ ܬܹܨܒܹܚ‑ܐܣܹܢ‑ܕ ܢ݁ܝܓ ܬܐܠܐ܃ ܐܿܪ ܬ݁‑ܬܘܥܝ ܐܲܪܐ ܬܹܪܓܐ: ܐܿܥ̰ܐܠܹܢ ܐܲܪ ܬ݁‑ܣ݁ܘܐܢ ܣ ܐܿܫܹܟ݁ܘܟ.
ܬܝܚ̰ܣܝ ܠܐ ܬܹܬ݁ܐܓܹܡ܃ ܐܼܦ̰ܹܠܹ݁ܩ ܘܘܠ‑ܝܣ܄ ܣܝ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ ܠܐ ܝܹܣ݁ܘܐ܃ ܝܹܕܹ݁ܟ݁ܝܪ!

ܬܹܘܹ݁ܨ̰‑ܕ ܠܥ̰ܹܠ݁ܐ: ܝܹܠ݁ܐ ܠܚ̰ܝܪ ܐܲܚ̰ܠܐܦ̰: ܠܘܝܢ‑ܕ܃ ܣܹ݁ܥ̰ܪܹܢ܃ ܕ݁ܙܹܢ܄ ܝܹܩ݁ܝܡ‑ܕ ܐܲܕ ܦ̰ܹܪܩܹܢ. ܝܹܕܹ݁ܡ‑ܕ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܬܐܨ̰ܹܠ݁ܐܥܬ܄ ܝܘܥ̰ܐܠ܃ ܡܝ ܝܹܟܬܐܠ ܣܹܬ݁ܐ ܐܼ ܝܝܡܐܢ‑ܝܣ܃ ܝܹܟܬܝܠ ܬܝܣ ܣܹܒܥܐ ܐܼ ܬܝܚ̰ܣܝ܃ ܝܝܢ'ܐܣ:
— ܐܲܕ ܬ݁‑ܬܐܘܝ ܥܹܡ݁ܬܝ܃ ܡܐ ܝܹܗܘܐ‑ܝܐܣ: ܢܫܐ‑ܠܹ݁ܗ܃ ܐܿܪ ܐܲܣ‑ܝܗܹܘ݁ܘ ܐܲܪܐ!

ܐܿܪ ܬܹܩܒܝܠ ܐܲܪܐ ܬܝܚ̰ܣܝ ܒܹܛ݁ܘ‑ܝܐܓܝ: ܬܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܕܥܐܥ̰‑ܟ ܣ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ܃ ܡܐ ܐܿܪ ܐܼܝܝ‑ܬܹܦ̰ܟܝܨ̰ ܫ݁ܪܹܥ.
ܝܹܦ̰ܟܐ‑ܝܐܣ‑ܬ. ܪܘܚܹܢ ܡܫܐܪܐܥܹܢ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܠܹܘܚܘܫ: ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣܹܢ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ:
— ܐܲܝ ܐܲܬ ܠܹܥܪܐܨ̰܃ ܐܲܡܹܟ ܐܲܪܐ ܕ ܐܲܣ‑ܦ̰ܟܹܥ̰ ܢܹ݁ܦ̰ܨ ܬܐܠ݁ܝ ܕ ܢܹܟ݁ ܐܼ ܕ‑ܝܹܬ݁ܐܓܡܹܢ܃ ܐܼܦ̰ܹܠܹ݁ܩ ܘܘܠ‑ܝܘ܉
— ܬܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣܹܢ: ܕ ܠܹܟܕܹܒ! ܕ ܣܝ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ ܐܿܡܝ ܢ‑ܬܹܣܠܐܡ ܠܐ ܝܹܕܹ݁ܟ݁ܝܪ: ܘܝܢ ܕ‑ܝܹܬ݁ܐܓܡܹܢ ܐܿܪ ܝܹܕܹ݁ܟ݁ܝܪ!

ܐܼܢܟܹܪ‑ܝܬ݁܃ ܐܲܒܐܕܹܢ!
ܬܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܬܪܘܚ ܬܹܘ݁ܝ‑ܕ ܐܿܫ݁ܐܝ ܕܝ ܬܹܝܠܹܘܬ܃ ܬܣܹܪܣ‑ܝܬ ܦ̰ ܫ݁ܦ̰ܹܪ ܢ ܘܹܢ݁ܐܪ. ܐܼܥ̰ܝܠ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܕ ܬܐܢܐܠܬ ܐܼ ܝܹܠ݁ܐܢ ܕܹܓ‑ܣ: ܐܼܩܹܕܹ݁ܡ ܐܲܕ ܕ‑ܝܹܕܹ݁ܡ: ܨ̰ܹܗܪܹܢܬ‑ܐܣ ܘܐܠܹ݁ܢ ܢ ܘܘܫ݁ܐܝ ܠܐ ܕ‑ܪܹܩܹ݁ܢܬ ܣܝ ܙܕܐܚ̰ܹܠ ܐܲܡ ܢܐܙܝܪ.

ܝܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܝܹܦ̰ܟܐ ܠܚܹܩ܃ ܝܹܪܢܐ ܠܒܐܛܹܠ: ܡܝ ܝܹܟܬܐܠ ܬܐܨ̰ܹܠ݁ܐܥܬ ܐܼ ܝܝܡܐܢ‑ܝܣ܃ ܝܹܟܬܝܠ ܣܹܬ݁ܐ ܐܼ ܬܝܚ̰ܣܝ܃ ܝܝܢ'ܐܣ:
— ܥܹܡ݁ܬܝ܃ ܡܹܣܟܝܢܬ܃ ܐܲܛܐܣ ܐܲܝ ܬܹܥܬܹܒ!

Translation.Title: The Wolf and the Ewe
Paragraphs: The wolf partnered with the ewe to cultivate a vegetable garden. He swore to her by God that he would not eat her, nor would he take her rightful share. They broke the ground, ploughed it again, and sowed beans. The rains fell, the crop grew, and it turned as green as the sea.

Summer arrived, and the plants began to turn yellow. They prepared to water them; however, the garden sat higher than the spring, and a trench could not reach it. Consequently, they had to water it using a pitcher.
The ewe kept fetching the water until her heart was bursting, while Sir Mḥemmed watered and sang contentedly!

The harvest season arrived, bringing an abundance of crop. They gathered it, dried it, and threshed it; all that remained was to divide it. The wolf took a large basket. After measuring out six portions for himself, he measured a seventh for the ewe, saying:
— My aunt can take this, if she likes: God willing, may it not satisfy her!

The ewe absolutely refused this division. She said to him:
— I appeal to you by God to grant me a trial.
He agreed. They went to seek judgment before the animals. The wolf said to them:
— Oh noble guests, how can I give half to her when I was the one fetching the water until my heart was bursting?
— She replied to them: It is a lie! It was Sir Mḥemmed whom you heard singing: anyone who is fetching water does not sing!

He denied it completely!
So she went and brought the hound inside a leather sack, placing it at the edge of the threshing floor. The wolf thought it was just a sack of grain resting there. He advanced to take it, but the eyes of the hound appeared, gleaming from inside like burning embers.

He quickly gave her what was fair and even what was not: while measuring one basket for himself, he measured six for the ewe, saying:
— My poor aunt, she labored so much!

Source.Title: ܐܿܫܹ݁ܢ ܕ ܐܼܙܝܡܹܪ
Paragraphs:
ܝܝܘ݁ܐܣ݁܃ ܝܹܡܠܐܠ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܕ ܐܼܙܝܡܹܪ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܬܹܪܓܐ ܢ ܘܐܡܐܢ.
ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ:
— ܡܪܹܚܒܐ ܝܝܣ݁‑ܟ܃ ܐܲ ܡ݁ܝܣ ܢ ܥܹܡ݁ܬܝ! ܕ ܐܲܫܘ ܟ‑ܝܕ‑ܝܹܘ݁ܝܢ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܕܐܓܝ܉
— ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܐܼܙܝܡܹܪ: ܕ ܦ̰ܐܕ ܐܲܝ ܦ̰ܘܕܹܥ̰܃ ܐܲ ܣܝ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ: ܐܿܣܝܥ̰‑ܕ ܐܲܕ ܣܘܹܥ̰.
— ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ: ܬܹܣܟܐܕ݁ܒܹܨ̰! ܟܪܐ ܕ݁ܐܘ ܐܿܩܹܪ݁ܘ‑ܟ! ܝܹܪܢܘ܃ ܝܹܡ݁ܐ‑ܟ ܬܹܫ̰݁ܐ ܠܚܹܩ‑ܝܘ ܢ ܠ݁ܘܒܝܐܢ: ܝܹܘ݁ܝ‑ܟ‑ܝܕ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ ܐܲܕ ܕ‑ܪܹ݁ܥ̰ ܬ݁ܐܪ‑ܝܘ!
— ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܐܼܙܝܡܹܪ: ܐܲܫܘ ܐܲܪܐ ܬܹܫ̰ܹ݁ܨ̰ ܕܹܓ‑ܝ܃ ܐܲ ܣܝ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ܉ ܡܘܩܹܠ: ܐܲܠܐ ܬܐܓܠܝܡܬ ܕ ܬܥ̰ܹܣܘܐܬܝܢ ܐܼ ܝܝ‑ܝܥܹܡܪܹܢ! ܣܹܒܪܘ‑ܝܝ ܟܪܐ ܢ ܘܐܓ݁ܘܪܹܢ܃ ܐܲܪ ܕ‑ܢܹ݁ܪܢܝܥ̰܃ ܐܲܕ ܕ‑ܩܹܘ݁ܝܥ̰: ܥܘܗܕܹܥ̰‑ܟ ܣ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ ܐܲܪܕ ܐܲܕ ܕ‑ܘܥ̰ܐܠܹܥ̰!
ܝܘܢܹܦ̰‑ܐܣ܃ ܐܼܪܘܚ. ܝܹܘܹ݁ܨ̰ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܝܹܡ݁ܐ‑ܣ܃ ܝܹܡܠܐ‑ܝܐܣ.

ܟ݁ܐܢ ܐܲܝܹܢ ܟ݁ܐܢ܃ ܘ݁ܝܢ ܐܿܫ݁ܐܝ ܕܹܓ ܝܹܣܢܝ܃ ܪܘܚܹܢ ܐܲܪܡܝ ܕ ܐܼܥ̰ܛ̰ܹܪ‑ܢ݁ܝ. ܐܲ‑ܬ‑ܐ ܝܘܣܐ‑ܕ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ. ܐܲܟܹ݁ܢ ܕ‑ܝܘܐܠܐ ܐܼܙܝܡܹܪ܃ ܝܹܙܡܘܡܹܓ ܕ ܬܐܨ̰ܣܐ: ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܟܹܫ̰݁ ܕ ܒܘ ܝܝܘܹܢ ܢ ܘܐܘܐܠ: ܬܘܣܝܨ̰‑ܕ ܐܲܕ ܟ‑ܫ̰ܹ݁ܥ̰…
— ܝܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܐܼܙܝܡܹܪ: ܓ݁ܐܠ݁‑ܝܝܝ ܦ̰ ܝܹܣܢܝ‑ܝܐܓܝ ܐܲܪ ܬܹܫ̰݁ܐ ܝܹܡ݁ܐ ܠܹܥܬܐܒ‑ܝܟ܃ ܬܹܫ̰ܹ݁ܨ̰‑ܝܝܝ.
ܝܹܪܦ̰ܹܕ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܬܐܩܹܙ̰݁ܝܪܬ‑ܝܣ܃ ܐܼܣܹܪܣ‑ܝܬ݁ ܦ̰ ܝܹܣܢܝ ܐܲܕ ܝܹܓ݁ܐܠ݁: ܝܹܡܹ݁ܥ̰‑ܕ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܐܣ ܘܘܫ݁ܐܝ܃ ܐܼܥ̰ܹܛ̰݁ܐ‑ܬ݁. ܝܹܒܕܐ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܠܐ ܝܹܣܟܹܥܘܝܘ܃ ܠܐܡܹܥܢܐ ܐܿܪ ܐܲܣ‑ܝܹܒܪܝ ܐܲܪܡܝ ܐܼܚܘܙܐ ܐܼܪܟܹܠ ܐܼܡܐܢ‑ܝܣ.
ܝܹܒܪܹܢ ܣܝ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܬܹܚ̰݁ܐܡܬ‑ܝܣ ܦ̰ ܬܠܐܬܐ ܐܼܨ̰ܐܪܹ݁ܢ: ܝܹܣܠܹܟ ܐܼܙܝܡܹܪ ܐܲܒܐܚܐܢ.

Translation.Title: The Wolf and the Lamb
Paragraphs:
One day, the wolf met the lamb near a stream of water.
The wolf said to him:
— Welcome, son of my aunt! What brought you here?
— The lamb replied to him: It is thirst, I am parched, oh Sir Mḥemmed: I came to drink.
The wolf said to him: You lie! There is something under your head! Furthermore, your mother ate my share of the beans: God brought you here so I can take my revenge!
— The lamb said to him: What could you possibly eat on me, oh Sir Mḥemmed? Look: nothing but skin and little bones fill my body! Grant me a few months until I grow and become strong: I swear to you by God that I will return!
He let him go, and the lamb went away. He reached his mother and told her everything.

Some time passed, and they carried the hound inside a large wicker basket, going down to that same ravine. Behold, the wolf arrived. As soon as he saw the lamb, he beamed with a smile and said to him:
— You are a man of one word: you have come so I may eat you…
— The lamb replied to him: Swear upon this wicker basket that my mother ate the reward of your hard labor, and then you may eat me.

The wolf raised his paw and placed it on the basket to swear: the hound lunged at it and bit it. The wolf began to yelp and howl, but the hound did not let go until the wolf had completely soiled himself.
Sir Mḥemmed turned back to his den on three legs; the lovely lamb was saved.

Source.Title: ܐܿܫܹ݁ܢ ܕ ܐܿܝܐܙܝܨ̰
Paragraphs:
ܝܝܘ݁ܐܣ݁܃ ܝܘܢܐܓ ܘܘܫ݁ܐܝ ܕ ܐܿܝܐܙܝܨ̰ ܐܼܢܝܓ ܐܲܡܹܩܪܐܢ.
ܨ̰ܐܠܹ݁ܢ ܐܼ ܐܼܕܘܪܐܪ ܕ ܐܼܥ̰ܐܠܹ݁ܢ܃ ܙܹܓܪܹܢ ܐܼܣܐܦ̰ܹ݁ܢ܃ ܩܹܓ݁ܠܹܢ ܕܝ ܬܥ̰ܹܙ݁ܐ ܕ ܬܠܘܬܐ. ܐܲܣ݁‑ܢ݁ܝ܃ ܝܹܥ̰ܠܝ‑ܕ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܐܣܹܢ ܝܝܨ̰ ܕܝ ܬܹܛ̰ܓܝ. ܐܲܝܐܙܝܨ̰ ܝܘܠܝ ܦ̰ ܬܐܣܐܦ̰ܬ ܕ ܬܐܥܠܐܝܐܢܬ: ܐܿܫ݁ܐܝ ܝܹܟܫܹܡ ܣ ܐܿܪܘܙ ܐܲܕ ܝܹܕ݁ܐܪܝ܃ ܝܹܩ݁ܝܡ ܕ ܐܲܥܹܣ݁ܐܣ.

ܐܲܟܹ݁ܢ ܕ‑ܝܙܹܘܹ݁ܩ ܠܹܦ̰ܙ̰ܹܪ܃ ܐܼܗܘܙ݁ ܐܿܝܐܙܝܨ̰ ܐܲܦ̰ܪܝܘܹܢ‑ܝܣ܃ ܝܹܒܕܐ ܠܐ ܝܹܣܥ̰ܘܓ݁ܘ. ܡܐܙܐܠ ܘܹܪܥܐܕ ܝܹܟܦ̰ܝ܃ ܝܹܘܹ݁ܨ̰‑ܝܬ‑ܝܕ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܠܓ̰ܹܕܪܐ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܬ݁ܒܐܪܝܟ ܠܹ݁ܗ ܕܝ ܬܐܥ̰ܹܫܬ ܐܼ ܟ‑ܝܹܦ̰ܟܐ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ! ܐܲ ܘܝܢ ܐܼ ܣ‑ܕ‑ܝܹܣܠܐܢ ܐܲܕ ܝܝܚܢܝܢ ܘܘܠ‑ܝܣ܃ ܐܲܕ ܝܹܙ̰ܹ݁ܡ ܬܐܛ̰ܐܠ݁ܝܬ: ܐܲܟܹ݁ܢ ܕ‑ܝܹܨܒܹܚ ܨ݁ܘܬ‑ܝܣ ܕܹܓ ܐܿܡܹܛ̰݁ܘܥ̰‑ܝܘ܃ ܢܕܹܟܘܐܠܹܥ̰‑ܕ ܣܹܓ ܝܝܨ̰ܹܣ܃ ܐܿܙ݁ܠܹܥ̰‑ܕ.
ܬܘܪܐ܃ ܐܲ ܠܚܐܓ̰܃ ܐܼܡܝ ܬܹܟܦ̰ܝܨ̰ ܬܘܕ݁ܢܐ܃ ܐܹܪܣ‑ܕ ܐܲܕ ܢܹܛ̰݁ܐܠ.

ܐܼܚ̰ܛ̰ܹܪ‑ܝܬ‑ܝܕ ܐܿܝܐܙܝܨ̰܃ ܝܹܦ̰ܗܹܡ ܒܹܠ݁ܝ ܡܐܫ̰݁ܝ ܕ ܛ݁ܐܥܐ ܢ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ ܐܼ ܬ‑ܝܕ‑ܝܹܘ݁ܝܢ: ܕ ܐܲܩܹܪ݁ܘ‑ܣ ܟܐܢ ܐܼ ܝܹܒܥ̰ܐ ܐܲܕ ܬ‑ܝܥ̰ܹܛ̰݁. ܝܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ‑ܕ:
— ܐܲ‑ܬ‑ܐܢ ܘܹܡܪܐܒܹܨ̰ ܕܹܓ ܘܘܪܘܙ: ܣ݁ܐܟܝ‑ܬ‑ܝܕ ܣܝ ܡܹܥܨ̰ܝܠ ܐܲܕ ܢ‑ܪܣܹܥ̰!

ܐܼܓܐ ܐܲܟ݁ܐ ܣܝ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ ܣ ܐܿܪܘܙ ܝܹܠ݁ܐܢ ܕܝ ܠܓ̰ܹܕܪܐ܃ ܐܼܨ̰ܹܗܪ‑ܐܣ ܘܘܫ݁ܐܝ ܝܹܛܹ݁ܣ: ܐܼܥܐܘܹܙ ܐܲܓ̰ܹܠ ܢ ܝܝܨ̰ ܕ ܐܲܥܹܣ݁ܐܣ܃ ܐܼܚܘܹܣ‑ܐܣ‑ܬܹܢܬ ܢܐܕܐܡ ܣ ܐܿܕܹܡ ܢ ܨ݁ܒܹܚ.
ܝܹܒܕܐ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܠܐ ܝܹܬܹ݁ܪܓܝܓܝ܃ ܝܹܩ݁ܐܪ ܐܼ ܐܿܝܐܙܝܨ̰:
— ܪܓ̰ܘ܃ ܪܓ̰ܘ! ܐܲܕ ܕ‑ܣܹܒܥ̰ܹܥ̰ ܠܘܨ̰ܘ ܐܲܕ ܕ‑ܘܥ̰ܐܠܹܥ̰!
ܝܹܢ݁ܣܹܪ ܐܲܡ ܘܹܙܪܹܡ ܕܹܓ ܐܿܣܐܥ̰ܘܪ܃ ܝܹܛܹ݁ܦ̰ ܐܲܒܪܝܕ‑ܝܣ܃ ܐܼܪܘܚ.

Translation.Title: The Wolf and the Rooster
Paragraphs: Once, the hound and the rooster went on a long journey. They looked out over mountains and ridges, crossed rivers, and halted in fields and vales. That day, night fell upon them in a forest. The rooster flew up onto a tall oak tree, while the hound went into a hollow space to shelter himself and remained there as a guard.

As the dawn began to color the sky, the rooster shook his wings and started crowing. Before he had even finished, the wolf came to the foot of the tree and said to him:
— Blessed be God for the voice He has given you! Whoever hears it, his heart will soften and he will perform his prayer. As soon as your voice struck my ear this morning, I woke up from my sleep and ran over.
Now, O Pilgrim, since you have finished the call to prayer, come down so that we may pray.

The rooster looked down at him and understood that it was not the devotion to God that had brought him, but that he simply wanted to crunch his head. He replied to him:
— The holy man is right there in the hollow. Wake him up while I come down!

Sir Mḥemmed looked toward the hollow in the tree and saw the hound sleeping: he had watched all night as a guard, and sleep had overcome him towards the morning.
The wolf began to tremble and said to the rooster:
— Wait, wait! Let me perform my ritual ablutions and I will return!
He slipped away like a snake into the dry grass, took to his path, and left.

Source.Title: ܐܼܙܹܡ ܕ ܘܹܪܓܐܙ
Paragraphs:
ܝܝܘ݁ܐܣ݁ ܐܼܪܘܚ ܘܹܪܓܐܙ ܣ ܐܿܫܹ݁ܢ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܐܲ ܣܝ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ܃ ܝܹܣܢܹܓܪ‑ܝܝܝ ܝܝܙܹܡ ܠܡܐܠ‑ܝܘ: ܐܿܪ ܐܲܣ‑ܙܡܝܪܹܥ̰܃ ܐܿܪ ܐܲܣ‑ܝܹܙܡܝܪ ܘܘܫ݁ܐܝ: ܐܲܕ ܬܨ̰ܹܒ݁ܪܹܨ̰ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܝ܃ ܐܲܕ ܐܲܟ‑ܦ̰ܟܹܥ̰ ܠܹܚܩ‑ܝܟ.
— ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ: ܝܹܠ݁ܐ ܘܐܪ܃ ܝܹܠ݁ܐ ܕܹ݁ܒ݁‑ܝܣ!
ܡܹܣܹܘ݁ܐܩܹܢ ܣ ܐܼܙܝܡܹܪ ܐܼܩܹܘ݁ܐܢ܃ ܡܥܐܗܐܕܹܢ ܣ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ ܐܿܪ ܡܝܹܚ̰ܕܹܥܹܢ.

ܝܹܫ̰݁ܘܪ‑ܕ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܬܐܝܠܹܘܬ ܢ ܬܝܙܝܬ ܬܐܬܝܛܘܚܬ ܝܹܬ݁ܝܠܝܢ ܕ ܐܼܓܹܠܦ̰ܐܢ ܕܹܓ ܘܹܠܡܐܬܹܢ. ܝܹܟ݁ܐܬ‑ܝܬ݁ ܝܝܙܹܡ ܣ ܬܘܥ̰ܡܐܣ‑ܝܣ܃ ܬܟܹܫ̰ܹ݁ܡ‑ܐܣ ܕܹܓ ܡܹܛ̰݁ܘܥ̰ܹܢ ܕ ܠܹܡܢܐܚ̰ܹܪ܃ ܬܹܣ݁ܘܦ̰ܘܥ̰‑ܝܬ ܣܝ ܠܥܹܩܠ‑ܝܣ ܘܐܠܐ ܣܝ ܬܹܛ̰ܓܝ܃ ܐܼܬܹܕ݁ܘ ܐܲܡ ܐܿܡܹܗܒܘܠ.
ܝܹܦ̰ܟܐ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܬܐܝܠܹܘܬ‑ܢ݁ܝ ܐܼ ܘܹܪܓܐܙ܃ ܝܹܣܡܐܪ‑ܝܬ݁ ܬܐܡܹܕ݁ܝܬ ܕܹܓ ܘܹܡܪܐܚ.
ܐܲܟܹ݁ܢ ܕ‑ܝܢܹܓܹ݁ܙ ܝܝܙܹܡ܃ ܝܘܦ̰ܐ‑ܕ ܬܝܙܝܬ ܬܹܫ̰݁ܘܪ ܐܲܦ̰ܪܐܓ. ܝܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܝܹܦ̰ܹ݁ܥ̰‑ܝܬ ܠܹܥܩܹܠ܃ ܝܹܛ̰ܹ݁ܠ ܐܲܡ ܐܿܙܹܩ݁ܘܪ܃ ܠܐ ܝܹܬܹ݁ܪܓܝܓܝ ܐܲܡ ܝܝܦ̰ܹܪ.
ܝܹܕܹ݁ܡ‑ܕ ܥ̰ܘܪ‑ܣ ܘܹܪܓܐܙ ܐܲܡܹܣܠܘܬ ܕ ܐܲܙܹܓܙܐܘ܃ ܝܹܟܹ݁ܪ‑ܐܣ ܐܲܪܡܝ ܐܼ ܣ‑ܝܹܣܹ݁ܘ݁ ܐܲܥܪܘܪ‑ܝܣ܃ ܝܘܢܹܦ̰‑ܐܣ܃ ܐܼܪܘܚ.
ܝܹܫܥܹܦ̰ ܝܝܙܹܡ: ܣܹܓ ܘܐܣ݁‑ܢ݁ܝ܃ ܐܿܪ ܕ‑ܝܘܥ̰ܐܠ.
ܥ̰ܐܣ ܐܲܪ ܬܐܡܹܛ݁ܘܬ܃ ܬܹܢ݁ܐ: ܕ ܠܥܐܠܝ ܣ݁ܘܩ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܝ! ܐܲܝܹܢ ܕ‑ܝܹܓ̰݁ܐ ܠܡܝܪ ܢ ܠܹܘܚܘܫ܃ ܐܲܕ ܬ‑ܝܟܹܡܹ݁ܠ ܣܝ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ!
ܬܘܥ̰ܐܠ܃ ܕܝ ܠܥܘܨ̰ ܐܲܪܐ ܬܹܪ݁܃ ܐܲܟܹ݁ܢ ܬ݁‑ܝܘܹܨ݁ܐ ܘܹܪܓܐܙ܃ ܐܼܙܝܡܹܪ ܕܝ ܬܹܝܠܹܘܬ܃ ܬܹܪ݁ܐ ܐܿܫ݁ܐܝ.
ܝܹܘ݁ܝ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܬܐܝܠܹܘܬ. ܐܲܪܡܝ ܕ ܐܲܒܪܝܕ ܝܹܣܬܹܥܦ̰ܐ܃ ܝܹܦ̰ܣܝ‑ܝܐܣ ܐܼܫܝܕ݁ܝ: ܝܹܦ̰ܹ݁ܥ̰‑ܕ ܥ̰ܘܪ‑ܣ ܘܘܫ݁ܐܝ܃ ܝܹܪܟܝ‑ܬ܃ ܝܹܣܚ̰ܹܢܙܹܪ‑ܝܬ ܐܼܪܟܹܠ.
ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܣܝ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ: ܠܚ̰ܝܪ ܡܹܣܨ̰ܝܪ ܕ ܐܲܩܕܝܡ! ܝܹܪܢܘ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܬ ܘܝܢ݁ܐ ܢ ܙ݁ܡܐܢ: ܬܐܡܹܠ݁ܐܠܬ ܢ ܬܡܹܛ݁ܘܬ܃ ܕ ܬܐܠܥ̰ܹܡܬ ܐܼ ܬ݁‑ܝܕ‑ܝܹܬ݁ܐܪܘܹܢ!

Translation.Title: The Lion and the Man
Paragraphs:
One day, the man went to the wolf and said to him:
— O Sir Mḥemmed, the lion is destroying my livestock. Neither I nor the hound can do anything against him. If you find a solution for me, I will give you your reward.
— The wolf replied to him: The lion exists, but so does his master!
The deal was struck over a plump lamb, and they swore by God not to betray each other.

The wolf filled a sack with those tiny stinging gnats that gather in swarms in the marshlands. When the lion snaps at them with his teeth, they get into his ears and nostrils, driving him out of his mind and out of the forest, making him run around like a madman.
The wolf gave that sack to the man, who emptied it in the evening inside the courtyard.
As soon as the lion leapt in, he found the courtyard full of gnats. He lost his senses, stretched out on the ground like a log, and began to tremble like a leaf.
The man grabbed a fresh wooden cudgel, went at him until he thoroughly thrashed his back, then let him go, and the lion left.
The lion was corrected; from that day on, he never returned.
As for the wife, she said to herself: More than I bargained for! What the king of the animals spared, Sir Mḥemmed will finish off!
Instead of putting what her husband had instructed—the lamb in the sack—she put the hound inside.
The wolf carried the sack away. Once on the road, he stopped to rest and untied the knot. The hound sprang out at him, mauled him, and tore him all over.
Sir Mḥemmed said: A good deed brings misfortune! Indeed, as the ancient saying goes: An egg belonging to the woman was laid by a female camel!

Source.Title: ܐܼܙܹܡ ܕ ܬܡܹܛ݁ܘܬ
Paragraphs: ܝܝܘ݁ܐܣ݁܃ ܬܹܪܦ̰ܹܕ ܬܡܹܛ݁ܘܬ ܬܐܩܐܒܐܫܬ܃ ܕ ܬܹܡܪܐܪܬ܃ ܬܪܘܚ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܬܹܛ̰ܓܝ ܐܲܕ ܕ‑ܬܹܙܕܹܡ. ܣܹܓ ܘܐܟܹ݁ܢ ܐܼ ܬ݁‑ܝܹܢܥ̰ܐ ܠܚܝܦ̰ ܢ ܝܹܣܥ̰ܐܪܹܢ܃ ܠܐ ܬܙܹܕܹ݁ܡ܃ ܬܹܬ݁ܪܘܛ̰ܘ܃ ܬܹܬܹ݁ܪ݁ܐ ܕܝ ܪ݁ܝܦ̰܃ ܐܲܪܡܝ ܬܹܣ݁ܐܘܹܨ̰ ܬܐܙܕܹܡܬ ܐܲܢܹ݁ܫܬ ܢ ܘܝ ܬ݁‑ܝܠܐ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ.
ܘ'ܐܪܐ ܬ݁‑ܝܫܝܕܹ݁ܢ܉ ܘ'ܐܪܐ ܬ݁‑ܝܣ݁ܝܘܨ̰ܹܢ ܣ ܐܲܚ̰݁ܐܡ܉ ܬܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܬܹܩ݁ܝܡ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܠܩܐܥܐ܃ ܬܹܛܹ݁ܦ̰ ܠܚܹܢܟ‑ܝܣ܃ ܐܲܪ ܬܹܬ݁ܚ̰ܹܡ݁ܝܡ.

ܝܘܦ̰ܐ‑ܬ݁‑ܝܕ ܝܝܙܹܡ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܐܲ ܝܹܡ݁ܐ ܬܐܡܥ̰ܐܪܬ܃ ܕ ܐܲܫܘ ܐܲܟ݁ܐ ܟܹܡ‑ܝܘܥ̰ܹܢ܉
ܬܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܬܹܚܟܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܠܚܝܦ̰ ܕܹܓ ܬܹܠ݁ܐ. ܬܹܚܟܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܐܼܪܟܹܠ܃ ܣ݁ܝܐ ܐܿ ܣ݁ܝܐ܃ ܬܹܪܢܐ ܬܹܚܟܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܬܐܡܣܐܠܬ ܢ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܕ ܬܹܝܠܹܘܬ ܕ ܬ݁ܐܪ ܐܼ ܣ‑ܬܹܪ݁ܐ: ܬܥ̰ܐܨ̰‑ܝܬ. ܝܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܐܼܫܐܕ݁ ܬܐܙܕܹܡܬ܃ ܝܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܬ݁ ܦ̰ ܘܹܥܪܘܪ‑ܝܣ܃ ܝܹܣܹ݁ܪܟܹܒ ܬܐܡܹܛ݁ܘܬ ܙܕܹܦ̰݁ܝܪ‑ܣ܃ ܪܘܚܹܢ ܐܲܪܡܝ ܬܐܘ݁ܘܪܬ ܢ ܘܹܚ̰݁ܐܡ.

ܬܐܡܹܛ݁ܘܬ ܬܹܣܹ݁ܟܫܹܡ ܬܐܙܕܹܡܬ܃ ܐܼܙܹܡ ܐܼܡܹܟܹ݁ܢ ܬܐܡܹܛ̰݁ܘܥ̰ܬ‑ܝܣ ܓܹܪ ܫ݁ܩܐܝܹܩ.
ܡ݁ܘܩܠܹܢ ܐܲܬ ܘܹܚ̰݁ܐܡ ܕܝ ܬܹܙܕܹܡܬ܃ ܡܐܫ̰݁ܝ ܕ ܐܲܝܹܢ ܐܲܪܐ ܕ‑ܬܣܹܠ݁ܟܹܨ̰: ܣܬܹܩܣܐܢ ܬܐܡܹܛ݁ܘܬ: ܬܹܚܟܐ‑ܝܐܣܹܢ. ܢ݁ܐܢ‑ܐܣ:
— ܕ ܐܲܫܘ ܐܲܪܐ ܬܝܢܝܨ̰ ܕܝ ܠܡܝܪ ܢ ܠܹܘܚܘܫ܉
— ܬܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣܹܢ: ܕ ܐܲܪܓܐܙ ܢ ܠܥܐܠܝ܃ ܡܹܥܢܐ ܐܼ ܝܹܬ݁ܦ̰ܘܚ ܢܹ݁ܦ̰ܣ‑ܝܣ!
ܐܲܟܹ݁ܢ ܝܹܣܠܐ ܝܝܙܹܡ ܐܼ ܘܐܢܹ݁ܫܬ‑ܐܓܝ ܝܹܢܹ݁ܚܫܐܡ܃ ܝܹܢܹ݁ܙܪܘܪܹܨ̰܃ ܐܼܪܘܚ.

ܐܼܥܹܕ݁ܐ ܘܐܝܹܢ ܐܼܥܹܕ݁ܐܢ܃ ܬܹܒܪܹܢ ܬܡܹܛ݁ܘܬ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܬܹܛ̰ܓܝ ܐܲܕ ܕ‑ܬܹܙܕܹܡ. ܝܐܦ̰‑ܝܬ݁‑ܝܕ ܝܝܙܹܡ: ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܘܹܬ‑ܝܝܝ‑ܕ ܣ ܬܩܐܒܐܫܬ ܣ ܐܲܢܝܝܪ!
— ܬܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ: ܐܿܪ ܙܡܝܪܹܥ̰: ܬܚ̰ܹܕܡܹܨ̰‑ܝܝܝ ܠܚ̰ܝܪ!
— ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ: ܐܲܕ ܐܼܝܝ‑ܕ‑ܬܹܘܬܹܨ̰܃ ܢܹܥ̰ ܐܲܕ ܟܹܡ‑ܫ̰ܹ݁ܥ̰.
ܬܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܬܹܘܬ‑ܝܬ ܣ ܬܩܐܒܐܫܬ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܓܹܪ ܘܐܠܹ݁ܢ. ܐܼܪܘܚ ܠܐ ܝܹܣܟܹܥܘܝܘ܃ ܝܹܙ݁ܐܙ݁ܐܠ ܐܼܕܐܡܹ݁ܢ.

ܟ݁ܐܢ ܐܲܝܹܢ ܟ݁ܐܢ܃ ܝܘܦ̰ܐ‑ܬ݁‑ܝܕ ܕܐܥ̰ܹܢ ܕܝ ܬܹܛ̰ܓܝ ܠܐ ܬܙܹܕܹ݁ܡ.
ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܐܲܢܝ‑ܝܝ‑ܕ.
ܬܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܐܲܪ ܐܲܣ‑ܬܹܬ݁ܐܢܝ܃ ܐܲܪܡܝ ܐܼ ܕ‑ܬܹܡܠܐܠ ܫ݁ܐܡܐ ܢ ܬܝܝܬܐ‑ܣ܃ ܓܹܪ ܘܐܠܹ݁ܢ. ܬܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܠܚܹܡܕܘ ܠܹ݁ܗ܃ ܐܲ ܡ݁ܝ܃ ܐܲܩܠ‑ܐܟ‑ܝܕ ܬܹܚܠܝܨ̰!
— ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ: ܠܹܓ̰ܪܘܚ ܩ݁ܐܙܹܢ܃ ܚܹܠ݁ܘܢ܄ ܐܼܡܹܣܠܐܝܹܢ ܩ݁ܐܙܹܢ܃ ܪܹܢ݁ܘܢ!
ܝܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܝܹܡܹ݁ܥ̰ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܐܣ܃ ܝܹܫ̰݁ܐ‑ܬ݁.

Translation.Title: The Lion and the Woman
Paragraphs: One day, the woman picked up a small axe and a rope, and went to the forest to gather wood. Because she was so worn out by the hardship of gathering firewood, she kept gathering, breaking, and setting it aside in a pile, until she had made a bundle as large as God could make it.
Who was going to bind it? Who was going to bring it home? So she sat back down on the ground, held her cheek in her hand, and fell into deep thought.

The lion found her there and said to her:
— O old mother, what is the matter with you?
She then related to him the hardship she was in. She told him everything, from this side and that, and she also recounted the matter of the wolf and the leather bag and the revenge she had taken for him; he felt pity for her. Then he bound the bundle of wood, placed it on his back, mounted the woman behind him, and they went all the way to the door of the house.

The woman brought the bundle of wood inside, while the lion placed his ear between the cracks of the door.
The people of the house looked at the bundle of wood—it was not something you could easily get away with bringing: they questioned the woman, and she narrated to them. They asked her:
— What do you say about the king of the animals?
— She told them: He is a good man, but how his breath stinks!
As soon as the lion heard this, he felt deeply ashamed, slunk away, and left.

After some time had passed, the woman returned to the forest to gather wood. The lion found her there and said to her:
— Strike me with the axe on the forehead!
— She replied to him: I cannot; you did a good deed for me!
— He told her: You will strike me, or I will eat you.
So she struck him with the axe right between the eyes. He left whimpering, making the blood run.

After some time had gone by, he found her again in the forest gathering wood.
He said to her:
— Delouse me.
So she began delousing him, until she came across the scar of her blow between his eyes. She said to him:
— Praise be to God, my son, you are healed!
— He said to her: Wounds dig and heal; words dig and multiply! Then he sprang upon her and ate her.

Source.Title: ܬܐܡܣܐܠܬ ܢ ܢܹ݁ܣܒܐ
Paragraphs:
ܝܹܘܹ݁ܨ̰ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܬܹܚ̰݁ܐܡܬ‑ܝܣ ܕܝ ܝܝܪ ܚܐܠܐ. ܬܕܝܘܐ‑ܬ ܬܘܫܹ݁ܢܬ ܓܹܕ݁ܐܫ ܕ ܘܐܡܹܟ ܝܹܚܠܐ. ܬܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܬܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܝ݁ܐ܃ ܐܲܝ ܐܲܪܓܐܙ܃ ܐܲܕ ܢ‑ܨ̰ܹܒ݁ܪܹܥ̰. ܐܼܨ̰ܐܢ ܕ ܐܲܬܡܐܬܹܢ‑ܢܹ݁ܥ̰: ܥ̰ܹܪ‑ܢܹܥ̰ ܐܲܩܫܝܫ܃ ܥ̰ܹܪ‑ܣܹܢ ܬܐܩܫܝܫܬ: ܐܲܕ ܬܹܢ‑ܢܣܹܡܝܹܙ̰ܘܐܓ̰܃ ܐܲܕ ܬܹܡܣܘ ܬܹܥܕܐܘܬ ܓܐܪ‑ܐܢܹܥ̰.
— ܝܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ: ܐܲܬܡܐܬܹܢ ܕ ܐܲܬܡܐܬܹܢ܃ ܐܲܥܹܒ݁ܘܨ̰ ܐܼܦ̰ܹܪܩ‑ܝܬܹܢ. ܐܿܪ ܐܲܥ̰‑ܬ݁ܢܐܣܐܒܹܢ ܐܲܪܐ.
ܐܲܪܡܝ ܐܼ ܬ‑ܬܹܚܪܹܣ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܪܘܚ ܟܹܡ݁ ܥܪܹܨ̰‑ܕ ܐܼܡܐܢ‑ܝܡ!

ܬܫܹܒܹ݁ܚ ܬܘܫܹ݁ܢܬ܃ ܬܢܐܘܹܠ܃ ܬܪܘܚ ܐܲܕ ܕ‑ܬܹܚ̰ܨ̰ܹܒ. ܐܲܟܹ݁ܢ ܬܹܘܹ݁ܨ̰܃ ܦ̰݁ܥ̰ܹܢ‑ܕ ܥ̰ܘܪ‑ܣ. ܬܒܹܪ݁ܐ܃ ܬܹܢ݁ܐ:
— ܕ ܢܹ݁ܣܒܐ ܢ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ ܐܼ ܝܝ‑ܕ‑ܝܹܘ݁ܝܢ!
ܐܿܪ ܐܲܣ‑ܣܹ݁ܡܚܹܣܹ݁ܢ ܐܲܪܐ: ܒܹܙܒܐܙܹܢ‑ܬ݁‑ܝܕ܃ ܐܼܪܘܚ ܢ݁ܘܐܠ‑ܢ݁ܝ ܕ ܐܲܒ݁ܘ܄ ܣܚ̰ܹܢܙܹܪܹܢ‑ܬ݁ ܐܼܪܟܹܠ: ܐܼ ܬ݁‑ܝܕ‑ܝܡܹܢܥܹܢ ܕ ܐܼܨ̰ܐܪܹ݁ܢ‑ܝܣ.
ܝܘܦ̰ܐ‑ܬ݁‑ܝܕ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܠܟܐܢܘܢ ܠܐ ܬܹ݁ܩܹ݁ܕ ܬܝܝܝܬܘܝܢ ܣ ܬܡܹܣ. ܝܹܡ݁ܘܩܹܠ‑ܝܬ݁܃ ܬܹܡ݁ܘܩܹܠ‑ܝܬ‑ܝܕ: ܐܿܪ ܐܲܣ‑ܝܹܢ݁ܝ܃ ܐܿܪ ܐܲܣ‑ܕ‑ܬܹܢ݁ܝ. ܬܹܪܘܐ ܪ݁ܐܝ‑ܝܣ ܘܹܚܕ‑ܣ.

Translation.Title: The Matter of Alliance
Paragraphs:
The wolf arrived at his den in a terrible state. The she‑wolf nursed him back to health through much effort. Afterward, she said to him:
— Come, husband, let me propose a plan. The dogs are our brothers: we have a boy, and they have a girl. Let us marry them to one another, and the enmity between us will be wiped away.
— He replied to her: Brothers are brothers, but the womb divides them. They will never accept an alliance with us.
Only when she relentlessly pressed him did he say to her:
— Go on then, try it yourself!

The she‑wolf dressed herself up, prepared a meal, and went out to propose the marriage. As soon as she arrived, they came out against her. She protested, saying:
— It is an alliance in the name of God that has brought me here!
They did not listen to a word she said: they fell upon her and tore at her, that prepared meal went up in smoke, and they all fiercely mangled her; she owed her survival only to her legs.

The wolf found her by the hearth, cauterizing her wounds with fire. He looked at her, and she looked back at him: he said nothing to her, and she said nothing to him. She had fully tasted the consequences of her own counsel.

Source.Title: ܠܡܘܬ ܢ ܘܘܫ݁ܐܝ
Paragraphs: ܝܹܩ݁ܝܡ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܕ ܝܝܡܐܢ‑ܝܣ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ: ܝܐ ܥܓ̰ܐܒܐ! ܠܹܘܠܹܓ݁ܐ ܐܼܪܘܚܹܢ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܢܹ݁ܣܒܐ ܢ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ܃ ܕ ܐܼܨ̰ܐܪܹ݁ܢ‑ܝܣ ܐܼ ܬ݁‑ܝܕ‑ܝܡܹܢܥܹܢ܃ ܬܐܠ݁ܝ ܘܝܣܹ݁ܢ ܐܲܫܘ ܐܲܪܐ ܝܝܕ‑ܣ ܝܹܨ̰ܪܘܢ! ܬܐܓܝ ܕ ܬܐܢܹܓ݁ܐܪܘܬ ܢܹܟ݁ ܕ ܘܘܫ݁ܐܝ.

ܐܲܝܹܢ ܝܹܟ݁ܐܢ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܐܣ ܐܼܪܟܹܠ܃ ܩܒܹܠ ܐܲܣ݁‑ܢ݁ܝ܃ ܐܿܪ ܐܲܣ‑ܝܚܘܠܦ̰ܐ ܐܲܟܹ݁ܢ ܐܼܚܘܠܦ̰ܐ ܐܼ ܣܹ݁ܪ ܕ‑ܝܹܬ݁ܘܐܟ݁ܣܹܢ ܦ̰ ܬܥܹܓ݁ܐܠܬ‑ܝܣ. ܣܹܓ ܘܐܟܹ݁ܢ ܐܿܪ ܐܲܣ‑ܝܹܙܡܝܪ ܐܲܪܐ ܐܼ ܘܹܓܕܝ ܣ ܝܝܥ̰ܝܠ‑ܝܣ܃ ܐܼܙ̰ܒܹܕ‑ܕ ܬܐܡܘܣܢܝ ܕ ܝܝܦ̰ܝܣ܃ ܐܿܕܐܝ! ܐܲܢܹܓ݁ܐܪܘ ܕܝ ܠܚ̰ܐܠܐܝܹܩ! ܐܿܥ̰ܐܠܹܢ ܕ ܐܼܡܹܕ݁ܘܟܐܠ܃ ܐܹܫ̰݁‑ܢ܃ ܬܹܫ̰ܹ݁ܨ̰‑ܕ.

ܝܝܘ݁ܐܣ݁܃ ܐܼܪܘ‑ܝܐܣ ܬܐܡܹܨ̰ܪܘܪܬ ܕ ܠܚܝܦ̰ ܝܹܟ݁ܐܢ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܐܣ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܐܲܕ ܐܼܝܝ‑ܬܥܝܘܢܹܨ̰ ܕܹܓ ܘܘܫ݁ܐܝ܃ ܐܲܕ ܕ‑ܪܹ݁ܥ̰ ܣܹܓ‑ܣ ܬ݁ܐܪ: ܐܲܕ ܐܲܟ‑ܦ̰ܟܹܥ̰ ܠܹܚܩ‑ܝܟ.
ܐܼܩܒܹܠ‑ܐܣ ܐܿܦ̰ܘܚܐܢ. ܥܐܣܹ݁ܢ‑ܬ ܐܲܪܡܝ ܕ ܐܲܣܡܝ ܐܼ ܣ‑ܘܦ̰ܐܢ ܐܲܣܘܠܹܦ̰܃ ܩܹܣܕܹܢ‑ܬ. ܐܿܫܹ݁ܢ ܝܹܣ݁ܠܹܩܨ̰‑ܝܬ‑ܝܕ܃ ܐܼܦ̰݁ܝܣ ܝܹܘܬ‑ܝܬ܃ ܝܹܢܥ̰ܐ‑ܬ: ܫ̰݁ܐܢ‑ܬ.

ܣ݁ܝܹܢ݁ܐ܃ ܢܹܗܪܹܢ‑ܕ ܠܡܐܠ܃ ܐܲܪܡܝ ܕ ܐܲܒܪܝܕ ܡܠܐܠܹܢ‑ܕ ܕ ܝܝܙܹܡ.
ܐܿܫܹ݁ܢ ܐܼܙ̰ܹܠܹ݁ܒ܃ ܝܹܪܘܹܠ. ܐܼܦ̰݁ܝܣ܃ ܝܘܥ̰ ܣܹܓ‑ܣ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ ܠܚܹܩ: ܝܹܘܬ‑ܝܬ ܝܝܙܹܡ܃ ܝܹܪܛ̰ܐ‑ܬ ܕܝ ܬܒܐܩܝܬ ܢ ܘܐܡ݁ܐܣ܃ ܝܹܓ̰݁ܐ‑ܬ. ܐܲܣܡܝ ܝܹܚܠܐ܃ ܝܹܢܩܹܣ ܐܿܨ̰ܐܪ‑ܝܣ ܝܹܩ݁ܝܡ ܕ ܐܲܥܹܘܛ̰ܐܠ܃ ܣܹܓܡܝ ܐܼ ܣ‑ܩ݁ܐܪܹܢ ܕ ܒܘ ܬܠܐܬܐ ܐܼܨ̰ܐܪܹ݁ܢ.

ܐܲܟ݁ܐ ܐܼ ܝܹܡ݁ܘܬ ܘܘܫ݁ܐܝ ܡܹܣܟܝܢ܃ ܝܹܬ݁ܥܐܣ݁ܐܢ ܠܡܐܠ ܐܲܓܘܓܐܡ.
ܐܼܣܹܘܹ݁ܩ ܕܹܓ‑ܣ ܓܡܐ‑ܣ܃ ܝܹܢܥ̰ܐ‑ܬ ܝܝܦ̰݁ܝܣ ܐܿܪ ܢܹܣܥܝ ܢ݁ܝܦ̰! ܣܹܓ ܘܐܣ݁‑ܢ݁ܝ ܐܼ ܝܹܢܕܹܩ ܠܚ̰ܝܪ.

Translation.Title: The Death of the Hound
Paragraphs: The wolf sat by himself and said: How astonishing! The delicate one went for an alliance in the name of God, and it was only her legs that saved her; who knows what could have happened to her! This is the end between me and the hound.

Of everything that had ever happened to him before that day, he had never felt anything like the blow to his honor regarding his wife. Because he was not strong enough to face the dog by brute force, he drew upon an acquaintance with the hyena —a wretched outcast! The lowest of all creatures! They became companions, eating together.

One day, he lamented to him the misfortune and hardship that had befallen him, saying:
— Help me against the hound so I can take my revenge on him, and I will give you your share.
The foul‑smelling beast accepted. They watched him until they found an opportunity, and they went after him. The wolf lured him out, and the hyena struck him down and killed him; they ate him.

From there, they drove away the livestock, until along the road they crossed paths with the lion.
The wolf leaped away and fled. As for the hyena, God took justice from him: the lion struck him, breaking the small of his back, and left him. When he healed, his leg was shortened and he remained lame, which is why people call him the three‑legged one.

That is how the poor hound died, he who used to guard the mute livestock.
His own brother plotted against him, and he was killed by the hyena who has no honor! It is from that very day that goodness vanished.

Source.Title: ܐܿܫܹ݁ܢ ܕ ܬܡܹܠܩܘܒܹܥܬ
Paragraphs: ܝܝܘܹܬ ܢ ܬܡܹܠܩܘܒܹܥܬ ܬܓܐ ܠܥܹܫ݁‑ܝܣ ܕܹܓ ܝܹܦ̰ܪܝ. ܬܘܪܹܘ ܕܹܓ‑ܣ ܬܹܙܕܹܠ܃ ܬܣܹܦ̰ܪܘܪܚ̰‑ܕ ܐܼܦ̰ܪܐܚ̰. ܣ݁ܝܹܢ܃ ܣܹܓܡܝ ܐܲܪܐ ܕ‑ܝܹܢܩܹܪ ܝܝܛܝܙ̰ ܐܲܠܐܡ݁ܐ ܝܹܥ̰ܠܝ ܕܝ ܠܹܒܚܹܪ܃ ܕܹܓ ܐܿܙܐܠ ܐܲܡ ܬܡܹܣ܃ ܢܹܬ݁ܐܬ ܐܲ‑ܬ݁‑ܐܢ ܬܪܘܚ܃ ܐܲ‑ܬ݁‑ܐܢ ܬܘܥ̰ܐܠ‑ܕ܃ ܬܹܣܹ݁ܠܩܐܨ̰ ܐܲܪ݁ܐܘ‑ܝܣ.

ܐܲܣ݁‑ܢ݁ܝ܃ ܐܼܥܹܕ݁ܐ‑ܕ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ܃ ܐܼܘܐܠܐ‑ܬ݁܃ ܝܹܣܠܐ ܐܼ ܝܹܦ̰ܪܐܚ̰‑ܝܣ ܠܐ ܫ̰ܹ݁ܘܫ̰ܝܘܹܢ. ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܨ̰ܹܓܹ݁ܪ‑ܕ ܝܝܘܹܢ܃ ܢܹܥ̰ ܐܲܪܕ ܢ‑ܐܠܝܥ̰!
ܬܹܒܕܐ ܬܡܹܠܩܘܒܹܥܬ ܬܝܝܝܬܐ ܢ ܠܝܙܐܪ܃ ܬܹܡܹ݁ܥ̰‑ܕ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܐܣ܃ ܐܲܕ ܬ‑ܬܹܢܩܹܒ. ܝܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܐܲܪ ܐܼܕܹܣ݁:
— ܡܐܫ̰݁ܝ ܕ ܣܝ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ ܐܿܡܝ ܬ݁ܟܹܠ݁ܝܚ̰ܹܢ! ܨ̰ܹܓܹ݁ܪ‑ܕ ܝܝܘܹܢ܃ ܢܹܥ̰ ܐܲܪܕ ܢ‑ܐܠܝܥ̰!
ܬܹܛܹ݁ܦ̰ ܝܝܘܹܢ ܣܝ ܬܩܹܙ̰݁ܝܪܬ܃ ܬܨ̰ܹܓܹ݁ܪ‑ܐܣ‑ܬ‑ܝܕ: ܝܹܫ̰݁ܐ‑ܬ܃ ܐܼܪܘܚ.

ܐܲܙܹܟ݁ܐ‑ܢ݁ܝ ܝܘܥ̰ܐܠ‑ܕ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܨ̰ܹܓܹ݁ܪ‑ܕ ܝܝܘܹܢ܃ ܢܹܥ̰ ܐܲܪܕ ܢ‑ܐܠܝܥ̰!
ܬܚܐܘܹܬ܃ ܬܪܘ܃ ܐܿܠܐܫ! ܬܹܛܹ݁ܦ̰ ܝܝܘܹܢ ܣܝ ܬܦ̰ܹܪܹ݁ܬ݁܃ ܬܨ̰ܹܓܹ݁ܪ‑ܐܣ‑ܬ‑ܝܕ: ܝܹܫ̰݁ܐ‑ܬ܃ ܐܼܪܘܚ.
ܬܹܩ݁ܝܡ ܬܡܹܠܩܘܒܹܥܬ ܠܐ ܬܹܬ݁ܪܘ ܐܼܕܐܡܹ݁ܢ܃ ܬܹܙ݁ܐ ܬܐܣܐ‑ܣ.

ܐܼܥܹܕ݁ܐ‑ܕ ܐܼܒܹܠ݁ܝܪܹܓ̰܃ ܝܘܦ̰ܐ‑ܬ݁‑ܝܕ ܕܝ ܝܝܪ ܚܐܠܐ. ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܕ ܐܲܫܘ ܟܹܡ‑ܝܘܥ̰ܹܢ܃ ܐܲ ܘܹܠܬܡܐ܉
ܬܹܚܟܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܦ̰ ܠܒܐܛܹܠ ܝܹܟ݁ܐܢ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܐܣ ܕ ܠܚܝܦ̰ ܕܹܓ ܬܹܠ݁ܐ.
ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܐܼܟܹܠܹ݁ܚ̰‑ܝܟܹܡ ܒܘ ܬܚܝܠܐ: ܠܘܟܐܢ ܝܹܙܡܝܪ ܐܲܕ ܢ‑ܝܐܠܝ܃ ܬܐܠ݁ܝ ܐܼ ܡ‑ܬܹܢ‑ܝܹܫ̰݁ܐ ܐܼܪܟܹܠ ܕܹܓ ܝܝܘܹܬ ܢ ܬܝܟܹܠܬ. ܠܐܡܹܥܢܐ܃ ܐܲܢܓܐ ܣ‑ܬܹܡ݁ܐܠܹܨ̰!
ܝܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܐܼܪܘܚ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܫܹ݁ܥ̰ܠ‑ܝܣ.

ܐܲܙܹܟ݁ܐ‑ܢ݁ܝ܃ ܝܘܣܐ‑ܕ ܣܝ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܨ̰ܹܓܹ݁ܪ‑ܕ ܝܝܘܹܢ ܢܹܥ̰ ܐܲܪܕ ܢ‑ܐܠܝܥ̰!
ܬܘܓܝ. ܐܼܥܹܫ݁ܐ ܝܹܣ݁ܐܓܐܕ܃ ܝܹܬ݁ܐܓܹ݁ܣ ܣ ܐܿܒܹܪܘܐܩ܃ ܝܹܬ݁ܫܹܒ݁ܝܒ ܕܹܓ ܝܹܦ̰ܪܝ: ܐܿܪ ܕ‑ܝܹܩܨ̰ܝ ܐܲܪܐ. ܬܐܡܹܠܩܘܒܹܥܬ܃ ܕ ܢܹ݁ܝ݁ܐ܃ ܬܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܪܘܚ ܦ̰ ܝܝܡܐܢ‑ܝܟ: ܝܹܟܦ̰ܐ ܐܿܟܹܠܹ݁ܚ̰! ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܝ ܥܹܡ݁ܝ ܐܼܒܹܠ݁ܝܪܹܓ̰ ܐܿܪ ܬܹܙܡܝܪܹܨ̰ ܐܲܪܐ ܐܲܕ ܕ‑ܬܐܠܝܨ̰: ܐܲܕ ܟ‑ܝܹܚ̰ܕܹܥ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ ܐܲܟܹ݁ܢ ܐܼ ܝܝ‑ܬܚ̰ܹܕܥܹܨ̰ ܕܹܓ ܘܐܪ݁ܐܘ‑ܝܘ!
ܝܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ:
— ܐܲܗ! ܕ ܒܘ ܐܼܥܹܙ̰ܩܘܪܹܢ ܐܼ ܟܹܡ‑ܝܹܣܚܹܪܫܹܢ܉ ܐܲܢܹܦ̰‑ܐܣ ܐܲܪ ܬ‑ܛ݁ܦ̰ܹܥ̰܃ ܒܘ ܐܼܥܹܦ̰ܢܐܨ̰: ܐܲܕ ܐܲܣ‑ܡܠܹܥ̰!
ܢܹܬ݁ܐ ܐܼܪܘܚ: ܬܐܡܹܠܩܘܒܹܥܬ ܬܥܹܓܹ݁ܢ‑ܐܣ ܐܼ ܐܼܒܹܠ݁ܝܪܹܓ̰.

Translation.Title: The Wolf and the Lark
Paragraphs: A certain lark made her nest in the hollow of a rock. She laid her eggs there in abundance, and hatched her chicks. From then on, from the rising of the sun until it set into the sea, in the midday heat like fire, there she was, going out and coming back, gathering food for her children.

That day, the wolf passed by, saw her, and heard her chicks chirping. He said to her:
— Throw one down to me, or else I will climb up!
The lark began her alarm cry, fluttering wildly down upon him to peck at him. Then the wolf began to laugh:
— It is not Sir Mḥemmed who is so easily fooled! Throw one down, or else I will climb up!
She took one of them by the leg and threw it down to him; he ate it and left.

The next day he returned and said to her:
— Throw one down to me, or else I will climb up!
She begged, she cried, but it was no use! She took one of them by the wing and threw it down to him; he ate it and left.
The lark remained there weeping tears of blood, her heart utterly broken.

The stork passed by and found her in a terrible state. He said to her:
— What is the matter with you, sister?
She related to him the injustice that had befallen her and the hardship she was in.
He told her:
— The trickster has fooled you! If he were able to climb up, he would have eaten them all at once. But whatever you do, do not show him that you know!
Then he went about his business.

The next day, Sir Mḥemmed arrived and said to her:
— Throw one down to me, or else I will climb up!
She refused. He tried everything to terrify her, making a show of climbing while rustling the asphodel stalks and scaling the rock, but he accomplished nothing. The lark, in her innocence, said to him:
— Go on your way; the fooling is over! Uncle Stork told me you are unable to climb up. May God betray you just as you betrayed me regarding my children!
The wolf replied to her:
— Ah! So it is that long‑legged one who made you clever? Just let me catch him, that eater of filth: I will show him!
He left, and the lark immediately sent warning to the stork.

Source.Title: ܐܼܒܹܠ݁ܝܪܹܓ̰ ܕ ܝܹܡܩܹܪܩܪܹܢ
Paragraphs:
ܐܼܪܘܚ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܣ ܐܼܡܩܹܪܩܪܹܢ ܐܲܕ ܐܲܣܹܢ‑ܕ‑ܝܹܣܹ݁ܒܓܹܣ܃ ܐܲܕ ܚ̰ܠܘܢ ܐܼܒܹܠ݁ܝܪܹܓ̰. ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣܹܢ:
— ܐܲܝ ܐܲܬܡܐܬܹܢ܃ ܝܹܫ̰݁ܐ‑ܕ ܬܐܣܐ‑ܢܘܹܢ ܐܼܒܹܠ݁ܝܪܹܓ̰: ܠܐ ܬ݁ܡܹܬ݁ܐܬܹܢ ܘܐܪ݁ܐܘ‑ܢܘܹܢ ܐܿܪ ܐܲܣܹܢ‑ܬܹܫ̰݁ܘܪ. ܐܲܡܹܟ ܬܩܹܒܠܹܡ ܫ݁ܥ̰ܹܠ‑ܐܓܝ܃ ܬܐܠ݁ܝ ܢܹܬ݁ܐ ܘܹܚܕ‑ܣ܃ ܟܹܢܘܝ ܐܿܪ ܟܹܢ‑ܝܟܹܦ̰݁ܘ ܐܲܪܐ ܐܿܙ̰ܹܢܘܝ܉ ܢ݁ܐܢ‑ܐܣ:
— ܐܼܚ̰ܘܨ݁‑ܐܥ̰ ܪ݁ܐܝ. ܨ̰ܹܒܹ݁ܪ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܐܥ̰܃ ܐܲ ܣܝ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ.
ܝܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܝܹܣܢܹܙ̰ܡܹܥ‑ܝܬܹܢ ܕܹܓ ܝܝܨ̰: ܘܬܹܢ ܠ݁ܘܥ̰ܐ‑ܢܣܹܢ: ܩܘܹܪ! ܩܘܹܪ! ܩܘܹܪ! ܡܟܘܠ ܝܝܘܹܢ ܝܹܡܹ݁ܣܠܝ‑ܕ ܐܲܝܹܢ ܕ‑ܝܹܡܹ݁ܣܠܝ܃ ܐܲܪܡܝ ܡܬܐܦ̰ܐܩܹܢ ܦ̰ ܝܝܘܹܢ ܢ ܘܐܘܐܠ: ܐܲܙܹܟ݁ܐ ܐܲܕ ܢܹܚ̰ܠܘ ܥܹܡ݁ܝ ܐܼܒܹܠ݁ܝܪܹܓ̰!

ܐܲܙܹܟ݁ܐ‑ܢ݁ܝ܃ ܒܹܓܣܹܢ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܠܦ̰ܹܬܢܐ܃ ܦ̰ܹܪܩܹܢ ܕ ܬܝܥ̰ܘܓ݁ܐ. ܐܲܟܹ݁ܢ ܕ‑ܝܹܪܣ ܐܼܒܹܠ݁ܝܪܹܓ̰ ܕܹܓ ܘܐܣܝܦ̰܃ ܩܹܕ݁ܡܹܢ ܥ̰ܘܪ‑ܣ ܣ ܬܝܛ̰݁ܝܦ̰ܬ. ܝܘܥ̰ ܠܚܐܠ܃ ܝܝܘܹܢ ܣܹܓ‑ܣܹܢ܃ ܕ ܒܐܒ ܢ ܢ݁ܝܦ̰܃ ܕ ܒܐܒ ܢ ܝܝܥ̰ܝܠ܃ ܝܹܙܘܐܪ ܙܕܐܬ‑ܣܹܢ ܐܲܡ ܐܿܓܹܠ݁ܝܕ ܙܕܐܬ ܠܹܡܚܹܠ݁ܐ. ܝܹܡܹ݁ܥ̰‑ܕ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܐܣ ܐܼܒܹܠ݁ܝܪܹܓ̰ ܣ ܐܿܡܹܢܩܐܪ‑ܝܣ܃ ܝܹܛܹ݁ܦ̰‑ܝܬ܃ ܘܹܚ̰݁ܪܹܢ ܘܝܝܐܨ̰. ܝܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܐܲܪ ܕ‑ܝܹܬ݁ܝܣ݁ܝܚ̰:
— ܐܲܒ݁ܘܗ! ܐܲܝ ܐܲܬܡܐܬܹܢ! ܐܲܢ݁ܐܥ̰܃ ܡܐܫ̰݁ܝ ܐܲܟ݁ܐ ܐܼ ܢܹܢ݁ܐ!
ܐܿܪ ܐܲܣ‑ܚܹܣܹ݁ܢ ܐܲܪܐ: ܪܹܘܠܹܢ ܣ ܐܼܡܹܪܙ̰ܐܢ‑ܢܣܹܢ܃ ܐܲܡ ܘܘܕܐܝܹܢ. ܡܟܘܠ ܝܝܘܹܢ܃ ܡܝ ܝܹܥ̰ܡܹܣ ܕܝ ܬܹܡܕܐ܃ ܝܝܢ'ܐܣ: ܐܲܡܫܘܡ ܒ ܪܐܣ‑ܘ! ܐܲܡܫܘܡ ܒ ܪܐܣ‑ܘ!
ܝܹܘ݁ܝ ܐܼܒܹܠ݁ܝܪܹܓ̰ ܒܐܒ ܢ ܢ݁ܝܦ̰‑ܢ݁ܝ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܠܥܹܫ݁‑ܝܣ܃ ܝܹܣܚ̰ܹܢܙܹܪ‑ܝܬ: ܫ̰݁ܐܢ‑ܬ ܘܐܪ݁ܐܘ‑ܝܣ. ܩ݁ܝܡܹܢ‑ܕ ܐܼܡܩܹܪܩܪܹܢ ܐܲܡ ܘܹܙܕܘܙ ܐܿܪ ܢܹܣܥܝ ܐܲܦ̰ܘܣ.

Translation.Title: The Stork and the Frogs
Paragraphs:
The wolf went to the frogs to rouse them, so that they would destroy the stork. He said to them:
— O brothers, the stork has eaten your very liver: your children are dying before their time is full. How can you accept this state of affairs, when he is all alone, while a whole valley would not be enough to contain you all?
They said to him:
— We lack wise counsel. Guide us, O Sir Mḥemmed.

So he gathered them together in the night: they struck up their language: croak! croak! croak! Each one spoke what they had to speak, until they agreed upon a single word: Tomorrow we will destroy Uncle Stork!

the next day, they equipped themselves for strife and divided into teams. As soon as the stork landed in the river, they advanced toward him with low croaking murmurs. As it happened, one among them, a master of honor and a master of strength, marched ahead of them like a king before his army. The stork lunged down upon him with his beak and seized him; the others drew back. Then he began to wail:
— Mercy, O brothers! By God, this is not what we agreed!
They did not listen to him: they fled back to their swamps, scattered like cowards. Each one, as they dived deep into the pool, said: Let the wretched one look out for his own head! Let the wretched one look out for his own head!
The stork carried that master of honor to his nest and tore him apart; his children ate him. The frogs were left behind like a mallet that has no handle.

Source.Title: ܐܿܫܹ݁ܢ ܕ ܐܼܒܹܠ݁ܝܪܹܓ̰
Paragraphs: ܐܿܪ ܐܲܣ‑ܝܓܝ ܐܲܪܐ ܐܼܒܹܠ݁ܝܪܹܓ̰ ܐܼ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܐܲܪܕ ܐܲܣ‑ܝܥܐܘܹܕ ܬܐܢܕܝܬ. ܐܼܥܐܣ݁‑ܝܬ: ܐܲܪܡܝ ܬ‑ܝܹܣܹ݁ܥ̰ܦ̰ܹܠ܃ ܝܹܡܹ݁ܥ̰ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܐܣ܃ ܐܼܚܘܙܐ‑ܬ ܣܹܓ ܐܿܣܹܠܣܘܠ ܐܿܙܐܓܘܪ܃ ܝܘܦ̰ܹܓ ܝܹܣ݁܃ ܐܼܪܦ̰ܹܕ‑ܝܬ ܕܹܓ ܓܹܢܘܐܢ.

ܐܲܪ ܐܼܬܹܢܹ݁ܨ̰ ܝܹܬ݁ܐܠܝ܃ ܐܼܬܹܢܹ݁ܨ̰ ܝܹܬ݁ܐܠܝ܃ ܐܲܪܡܝ ܐܼ ܕ‑ܝܚ̰ܹܠ݁ܐ ܐܼܕܘܪܐܪ ܥܠܐܝܹܢ. ܐܼܡܝܪܹܢ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܕ ܐܲܫܘ ܬܘܐܠܐܨ̰܃ ܐܲ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ܉
— ܝܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ‑ܕ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ: ܐܼܕܘܪܐܪ܃ ܐܼܙܘܥ̰ܐܪ܃ ܐܼܣܐܦ̰ܹ݁ܢ: ܐܲ‑ܬܹܢ‑ܐ ܐܼܪܟܹܠ ܕ݁ܐܘܐ‑ܬܢܹܥ̰!
ܝܹܪܢܐ ܝܘܠܝ ܝܹܣ݁܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܕ ܐܲܫܘ ܬܘܐܠܐܨ̰܉
— ܝܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ‑ܕ: ܝܹܥ̰ܠܝ‑ܕ ܫܐܠܘܐܘ ܦ̰ ܘܐܠܹ݁ܢ‑ܝܘ: ܐܿܪ ܦ̰ܪܝܙܹܥ̰ ܐܲܪܐ ܡܠܝܚ ܬܐܡܘܪܬ!
ܝܹܪܢܐ ܝܘܠܝ ܝܝܣ݁܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܐܼ ܬܘܪܐ܃ ܐܲܫܘ ܬܘܐܠܐܨ̰܉
— ܝܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ‑ܕ: ܢܚ̰ܹܠ݁ܐ‑ܕ ܐܲܣܝܓܢܐ!

ܐܼܡܝܪܹܢ܃ ܝܹܒܪܐ‑ܝܐܣ‑ܕ ܐܼܒܹܠ݁ܝܪܹܓ̰ ܐܼ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ: ܐܲܕ ܕ‑ܝܹܥ̰ܠܝ ܣܝ ܬܝܣ ܣܹܒܥܐ܃ ܐܲܕ ܝܹܩܒܹܪ܃ ܐܲܕ ܝܹܡܹ݁ܬ.
ܐܲܪ ܕ‑ܝܬܹܢܹ݁ܨ̰ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ܃ ܐܼܥ̰ܹܠ݁ܝ‑ܕ܃ ܐܼܬܹܢܹ݁ܨ̰‑ܕ ܐܼܥ̰ܹܠ݁ܝ‑ܕ܃ ܐܲܪܡܝ ܬܐܣܐ‑ܣ ܬܹܟܦ̰ܐ܃ ܐܲܨ̰ܝܚܐܢ ܝܹܒܨ̰ܐ ܣܝ ܠܚ̰ܘܦ̰.
ܝܹܦ̰ܹ݁ܥ̰‑ܝܬ ܠܹܥܩܹܠ: ܝܹܬ݁ܘ ܣܝܕܝ ܥܹܒܕܹܠܩܐܕܹܪ܃ ܠܐ ܣ‑ܝܹܩ݁ܐܪ:
'' ܐܲ ܣܝܕܝ ܥܹܒܕܹܠܓܹܪܢܝܢ!''
'' ܕܝ ܬܹܡܕܐ ܢܹܥ̰ ܕܹܓ ܘܐܠܝܡ!''
'' ܐܲ ܣܝܕܝ ܥܹܒܕܹܠܓܹܪܢܝܢ''
'' ܕܝ ܬܹܡܕܐ ܢܹܥ̰ ܕܹܓ ܘܐܠܝܡ!''

ܝܹܛܹ݁ܪܨ̰ܩ‑ܕ ܕܝ ܬܹܡܕܐ: ܐܿܦ̰ܓܹܢ ܘܐܡܐܢ ܣ ܐܼܓܹܢ݁ܝ܄ ܝܹܣܠܹܟ ܣܝ ܠܡܘܬ܃ ܠܐܡܹܥܢܐ ܬܹܟ݁ܐ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܐܣ ܬܟܹܦ̰݁ܐܪܬ!
ܝܹܫܥܹܦ̰: ܣܹܓ ܘܐܣ݁‑ܢ݁ܝ܃ ܐܿܪ ܕ‑ܝܹܫܥ̰ܝܠ ܕ ܐܼܒܹܠ݁ܝܪܹܓ̰.

Translation.Title: The Wolf and the Stork
Paragraphs: The stork did not give the wolf time to prepare another trap for him. He watched him until he caught him off guard, lunged at him, gripped him by the spine of his back, flew up with him, and carried him into the heavens.

He kept circling and rising, circling and rising, until he had left the high mountains far below. Then, he said to him:
— What do you see, O Mḥemmed?
— The wolf replied to him: The mountains, the plains, the rivers—there they all are beneath us!
He rose with him even higher and said to him:
— What do you see?
— He replied to him: A dimness has fallen over my eyes; I can no longer make out the land clearly!
He rose with him even higher and said to him:
— And now, what do you see?
— He replied to him: We have left the clouds behind!

Right then, the stork let go of the wolf, so that he would fall from the seventh heaven, smash to pieces, and die.
The wolf kept twisting as he fell, twisting as he fell, until his liver was spent and his spleen burst from sheer terror.
He lost his mind completely: forgetting Saint Abdelqader, he kept crying out to him:
'' O Saint Abdelgernin!''
'' In a pool or in the straw!''
'' O Saint Abdelgernin!''
'' In a pool or in the straw!''

He burst right into a pool, and the waters splashed all the way up into the sky. He escaped death, but what a severe penance he had endured!
He had learned his lesson: from that day forward, he never troubled himself with the stork again.
'''ܬܐܡܐܫܐܗܘܬ ܢ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܕ ܝܝܙܹܡ'''
'''The Tale of the Wolf and the Lion'''

Source.Title: ܠܹܩܪܐܝܐ ܢ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ
Paragraphs: ܝܹܦ̰ܹ݁ܥ̰‑ܕ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܣܝ ܬܹܡܕܐ ܠܐ ܝܹܬܹ݁ܪܓܝܓܝ ܐܲܡ ܝܝܦ̰ܹܪ. ܬܹܟܦ̰ܐ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܐܣ ܕ݁ܘܢܝܬ ܣܝ ܬܘܓܕܝ ܕ ܐܿܣܹܡ݁ܝܨ̰.

ܝܘܦ̰ܐ ܐܲܥ̰ܹܪܒܐܠ ܕ ܐܲܩܕܝܡ܃ ܝܘܥ̰ܐܠ܃ ܐܲܟܹ݁ܢ ܐܼܘܐܠܐ ܬܝܠܹܦ̰ܬ܃ ܝܹܛܹ݁ܦ̰‑ܝܬ ܕ ܐܲܡܹܢܕܐܝܹܪ܃ ܝܹܒܕܐ ܬܝܝܝܬܐ:
''     ܬܐ ܬܹܦ̰ܠܐ܃ ܬܐ ܐܿܪ ܬܹܦ̰ܠܝ:''
''     ܕ ܐܲܙ̰ܕܝܕ ܐܼ ܘܹܪ ܢܘܦ̰ܝ!''

ܬܘܐܠܐ‑ܬ‑ܝܕ ܬܝܠܹܦ̰ܬ ܠܐ ܝܹܬܹ݁ܪܓܝܓܝ܃ ܝܹܕܹ݁ܟ݁ܝܪ܃ ܐܲܡ ܘܝܢ ܐܲܪܐ ܬܹܪܟܹܒ ܠܝܚܐܠܐ܄ ܬܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ‑ܕ:
— ܬܹܥ̰ܪܝܨ̰܃ ܐܲ ܣܝ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ܉
— ܝܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ: ܐܲ ܡ݁ ܐܿܚ̰ܹܢܦ̰ܘܦ̰܃ ܐܲ ܡ݁ ܐܿܙܹܢܦ̰ܘܦ̰! ܐܿܪ ܬܹܛ̰ܪܝܨ̰ ܐܲܪܐ ܢܹܟ݁ ܥ̰ܪܝܥ̰: ܒܐܒܐ ܝܹܥ̰ܪܐ܃ ܙ̰ܹܕ݁ܝ ܝܹܥ̰ܪܐ. ܐܲ‑ܬ݁‑ܐܢ ܬܩܘܒܹ݁ܬ݁‑ܝܣ ܕܹܓ ܝܝܥ̰ܝܠ ܐܼܢ݁ܐ!

ܬܘܡܹܢ‑ܝܬ ܬܝܠܹܦ̰ܬ. ܦ̰ܪܐܢ ܐܲܕ ܐܲܣ‑ܝܹܣܥ̰ܹܪ ܐܲܪ݁ܐܘ‑ܝܣ܃ ܐܼܪܹܒ݁ܝ‑ܬܹܢ: ܐܲܕ ܐܲܣ‑ܬܹܦ̰ܟ ܠܚܹܩ ܢ ܠܹܥܬܐܒ‑ܝܣ. ܬܹܘ݁ܝ‑ܝܐܣ‑ܬܹܢ‑ܝܕ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܠܥ̰ܐܪ‑ܝܣ: ܕܝ ܬܢܐܫ ܝܝܕ‑ܣܹܢ܃ ܕ ܐܼܒܹܠܟܘܟܹܢ: ܡܝ ܬܹܡ݁ܘܩܹܠ ܕܹܓ‑ܣܹܢ ܝܹܡ݁ܐܬܣܹܢ܃ ܐܲܕ ܝܹܓ̰݁ܘܓ̰ܹ݁ܓ ܘܘܠ‑ܝܣ ܬܹܫ̰݁ܐ ܬܹܣܘܐ.

ܝܹܣܹ݁ܠܦ̰‑ܐܣܹܢ ܐܼܪܟܹܠ ܣܝ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ ܝܝܘܹܢ ܝܝܘܹܢ܄ ܐܲܪܡܝ ܝܹܟܦ̰ܐ܃ ܐܼܒܹܪ݁ܐ ܕܝ ܬܝܠܹܦ̰ܬ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܐܲ ܠܐܠ݁ܐ܃ ܐܼܘܐܟܹ݁ܢ ܐܲܝ ܥ̰ܪܹܢ ܘܐܪ݁ܐܫ܃ ܐܿܪ ܕ‑ܬ݁ܪܘܚܘ ܐܲܪܐ ܐܲܕ ܬܹܢ‑ܬܹܬ݁ܫܹܘ݁ܝܠܹܨ̰ ܟܘܠ݁ ܐܲܣ݁: ܡܝ ܣܹܢ‑ܕ‑ܬܹܘ݁ܝܨ̰ ܐܲܥܘܝܢ܃ ܐܹܦ̰ܟ‑ܝܝܝ‑ܬ‑ܝܕ ܕܹܓ ܡܝ ܢ ܬܹܘ݁ܘܪܬ܃ ܬܪܘܚܹܨ̰.
— ܬܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ: ܝܝܪܒܹܚ!
ܬܪܘܚ ܬܹܓ̰݁ܐ ܐܲܪ݁ܐܘ‑ܝܣ܃ ܐܲܠܹ݁ܢ‑ܝܣ ܠܐ ܬ݁ܒܹܥܪܘܪܘܫܹܢܬ ܕ ܐܼܡܹܛ݁ܐܘܹܢ.
ܝܹܒܪܹܢ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܦ̰ ܘܐܪ݁ܐܘ ܢ ܬܝܠܹܦ̰ܬ܃ ܝܹܫ̰݁‑ܝܬܹܢ.
ܝܹܪ݁ܐ ܐܼܥ̰ܣܐܢ‑ܢܣܹܢ ܕܝ ܬܹܒܨ̰ܐܢܝܢ‑ܢܣܹܢ܃ ܐܼܥܹܠܹ݁ܩ‑ܝܬܹܢܬ܃ ܐܲܪ ܬ݁ܛ̰ܹܢܛ̰ܘܢܹܢ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܐܣܹܢܬ ܐܼܓܹܠܦ̰ܐܢ ܢ ܘܐܪܹܛ̰ܹ݁ܢ ܕ ܝܝܙܐܢ ܐܼܙܹܓܙܐܘܹܢ.

ܡܝ ܕ‑ܬܒܹܕ݁ ܬܝܠܹܦ̰ܬ ܣ ܘܹܥܘܝܢ܃ ܝܝܢ'ܐܣ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ:
— ܣܹܠ! ܣܹܠ! ܐܲܟܹ݁ܢ ܠܐ ܩ݁ܐܪܹܢ܃ ܣܹܠ!

ܐܲܣ݁‑ܢ݁ܝ܃ ܬܹܙ̰ܹ݁ܡ‑ܝܬܹܢ܃ ܐܿܪ ܬ݁‑ܬܗܹܢ݁ܐ ܐܲܪܐ ܬܐܣܐ‑ܣ܃ ܬܹܕܗܹܡ ܐܲܕ ܬܹܢ‑ܬܛ̰ܹܪ: ܬܘܦ̰ܐ‑ܢ ܐܲܝܹܢ ܬܘܦ̰ܐ! ܐܼܢܹܓܹ݁ܙ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ܃ ܝܹܪܘܹܠ ܕܝ ܠܥ̰ܐܪ: ܬܹܬܒܹܥ‑ܝܬ ܬܝܠܹܦ̰ܬ܃ ܬܹܛܹ݁ܦ̰‑ܝܬ ܣܹܓ ܐܿܨ̰ܐܪ ܕܝ ܛ݁ܠܐܡ. ܝܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܐܲܪ ܐܼܕܹܣ݁܃ ܝܹܩ݁ܐܪ‑ܐܣ:
— ܐܿܗ! ܬܹܛܹ݁ܦ̰ ܐܲܛ̰ܐܪ܃ ܬܥ̰ܝܠ ܕ ܐܲܨ̰ܐܪ! ܬܹܛܹ݁ܦ̰ ܐܲܛ̰ܐܪ܃ ܬܥ̰ܝܠ ܕ ܐܲܨ̰ܐܪ!
ܐܼܟܹܠܹ݁ܚ̰‑ܐܣ܃ ܬܹܒܪܐ‑ܝܐܣ܃ ܝܹܪܘܹܠ܃ ܝܹܦ̰ܹ݁ܥ̰ ܣܝ ܠܓ̰ܝܗܐ ܢ݁ܝܨ̰ܹܢ܃ ܝܹܡܢܹܥ.

Translation.Title: The Wolf's Education
Paragraphs: The wolf came out of the pool trembling like a leaf. The world had turned upside down for him from sheer terror and cold.

He found an old sieve. Seeing the sow approaching, he held it like a frame drum and began to beat it, singing:
''     This hole is pierced, that one is not:''
''     We could not find anything newer!''

The sow saw him trembling and muttering as if possessed by a mystical trance. She asked him:
— Are you educated, O Sir Mḥemmed?
— He replied to her: O snout‑mouth, O muzzle‑snout! Do you not know that I am educated? My father was educated, and my grandfather was educated. Look, there is his domed shrine over on that hill!

The sow believed him. They agreed that he would teach her children and raise them, and she would pay him for his labor. She brought them to his cave: all twelve of them, plump little piglets. Whenever their mother looked at them, her heart bloomed with joy as if she had eaten and drunk her fill.

Sir Mḥemmed stroked every single one of them. When he finished, he washed his hands of the sow and said to her:
— Noble lady, for the children to learn well, you must not come and disturb them every day. When you bring their provisions, leave them right at the threshold of the door and go.
— She told him: Agreed!
She left her children behind, her eyes blurring with heavy tears.
The wolf turned upon the sow's children and ate them all.
He placed their bones inside their hollow skins and hung them up. Swarms of wasps and green flies began to buzz all over them.

Whenever the sow stood outside with the provisions, the wolf would say to her:
— Listen! Listen! Hear how they are reciting! Listen!

One day, she missed them too much and her heart could not rest. She rushed inside to see them, and she found what she found! The wolf leaped away and fled deeper into the cave. The sow pursued him and caught him by the leg in the darkness. He began to laugh, saying:
— Oh! She grabbed a root and thought it was a leg! She grabbed a root and thought it was a leg!
He tricked her. She let go, and he fled out through the other side and escaped safely.

Source.Title: ܐܼܙܹܡ ܕ ܬܝܠܹܦ̰ܬ
Paragraphs: ܐܲܪ݁ܐܘ‑ܝܣ ܡܹ݁ܫ̰ܹ݁ܢ܃ ܐܿܫܹ݁ܢ ܐܼܡܹܢܥ‑ܐܣ܃ ܬܹܩ݁ܝܡ ܬܝܠܹܦ̰ܬ ܠܐ ܬܹܬ݁ܪܘ ܐܲܡ ܠܹܗܘܐ܃ ܬܹܙ݁ܐ ܬܐܣܐ‑ܣ. ܐܲܫܘ ܐܲܪܐ ܬܹܚ̰ܕܹܡ܉ ܐܲܫܘ ܐܿܪ ܬܚ̰ܹܕܹ݁ܡ܉

ܬܪܘܚ ܐܲܕ ܬܫܹܬܟܝ ܐܼ ܝܝܙܹܡ܃ ܠܡܝܪ ܢ ܠܹܘܚܘܫ܃ ܬܹܚܟܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܐܲܡܹܟ ܐܼ ܣ‑ܝܟܹܠܹ݁ܚ̰ ܣܝ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ ܐܲܪܡܝ ܐܼ ܣ‑ܬܹܦ̰ܟܐ ܐܲܪ݁ܐܘ‑ܝܣ ܥܙܝܙܹܢ ܐܲܕ ܬܹܢ‑ܝܹܣܥ̰ܹܪ܃ ܐܲܡܹܟ ܐܼ ܬ‑ܬܹܣ݁ܥܐܫ ܓܹܕ݁ܐܫ܃ ܐܲܡܹܟ ܐܼ ܬܹܢ‑ܝܹܫ̰݁ܐ܃ ܐܲܡܹܟ ܐܼ ܣ‑ܝܹܡܢܹܥ. ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܝܝܙܹܡ:
— ܐܲ ܝܹܠ݁ܝ܃ ܣܝ ܙܝܟ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ ܕ ܐܲܥ̰ܹܕ݁ܐܪ. ܢܹܠ݁ܐ ܢܨܹܓܹ݁ܡ ܕ݁ܘܢܝܬ܃ ܝܹܣܚ̰ܹܨܪ‑ܐܢܹܥ̰‑ܬ݁. ܐܲܕ ܬ‑ܬܹܚ̰ܕܹܥ ܬܓܹܠ݁ܐ ܕ ܠܹܡܠܹܚ ܐܼ ܣ‑ܬܹܣܹ݁ܫ̰ܹ݁ܨ̰!
ܝܹܪܛ̰ܐ ܠܹܥܗܘܕ ܢ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ܃ ܐܲܦ̰ܘܣ‑ܝܣ ܐܲܕ ܬ‑ܝܹܛܹ݁ܦ̰! ܐܿܪ ܬ݁ܐܓܐܕ: ܐܲܕ ܐܲܡ‑ܪܹ݁ܥ̰ ܬ݁ܐܪ.

ܝܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܠܐܡܹܥܢܐ܃ ܢܹܟ݁ ܠ݁ܘܛ̰ܹܥ̰: ܐܲܕ ܬܥܹܡܠܹܨ̰ ܕܹܓ‑ܝ ܠܹܡܙܹܓ݁ܐ܃ ܐܲܕ ܐܼܝܝ‑ܬܹܦ̰ܟܹܨ̰ ܐܲܩܹܪ݁ܘ‑ܡ ܐܲܕ ܬ‑ܥ̰ܹܛ̰ܹ݁ܥ̰: ܐܲܕ ܐܲܡ‑ܦ̰ܟܹܥ̰ ܬܐܨܘܝܥܬ ܐܼܒܐܘܹܢ ܣ ܐܲܢܹܒܕܘ.

ܬܝܠܹܦ̰ܬ ܬܚܹܡܹ݁ܠ ܐܼܒܐܘܹܢ: ܬܹܣܹ݁ܡܚܹܣ܃ ܘܐܠܐܟܝܢ܃ ܣܹܓ ܘܐܣܡܝ ܐܼ ܬ݁‑ܝܹܥ̰ܕܹܪ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܕܹܓ ܘܐܪ݁ܐܘ‑ܝܣ܃ ܠܐܡܐܢ ܘ݁ܝܢ‑ܬ ܘܐܡܐܢ.
ܬܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܐܲ ܠܡܝܪ ܢ ܠܹܘܚܘܫ܃ ܢܹܟ݁ ܐܲܩܠ‑ܝ ܕܝ ܝܝܪ ܚܐܠܐ: ܐܲܕ ܐܼܝܝ‑ܬܐܢܦ̰ܹܨ̰ ܐܲܪܕ ܩ݁ܝܡܹܥ̰ ܕ ܝܝܡܐܢ‑ܝܘ: ܫܘܒܟܹܥ̰‑ܟ ܣ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ ܐܲܪܕ ܐܲܕ ܕ‑ܘܥ̰ܐܠܹܥ̰܃ ܐܲܕ ܐܲܟ‑ܕ‑ܪܹ݁ܥ̰ ܣ ܠܹܚ̰ܒܐܪ.
ܝܘܢܹܦ̰‑ܐܣ ܬܪܘܚ.

Translation.Title: The Lion and the Sow
Paragraphs: Her children had been eaten and the wolf had escaped her; the sow remained there weeping like the rain, her heart utterly broken. What was she to do? What was she not to do?

She went to complain to the lion, the king of the animals, and she recounted to him how Sir Mḥemmed had tricked her until she gave him her beloved children to educate, how much she had provided for his livelihood, how he had eaten them, and how he had escaped her. The lion said to her:
— My daughter, since olden times Mḥemmed has been a traitor. We had set the world in order, and he ruined it for us. May the bread and the salt you fed him betray him! He has broken the covenants of God; His hand will surely seize him! Do not fear: I will take revenge for you.

Then he said to her:
— However, I am hungry: if you would do me a favor, give me your head to chew on, and I will give you a measure of broad beans in the summer.

The sow loved broad beans: she listened to the offer, but ever since the wolf had betrayed her regarding her children, trust had been carried away by the waters.
She replied to him:
— O king of the animals, I am in a terrible state: leave me be until I can compose myself. I bind you by God that I will return and bring you word.
He let her go, and she departed.

Source.Title: ܐܿܫܹ݁ܢ܃ ܕ ܬܝܠܹܦ̰ܬ ܕ ܝܝܙܹܡ
Paragraphs: ܐܿܫܹ݁ܢ ܝܹܛ̰ܪܐܢ ܬܝܢ ܝܹܚ̰ܕܹܡ ܠܐ ܐܼ ܝܝܙܹܡ ܘܐܠܐ ܐܼ ܬܝܠܹܦ̰ܬ܃ ܝܹܬ݁ܐܓܐܕ ܣܝ ܬܝܠܝ‑ܣ. ܐܲܡܹܟ ܐܲܪܐ ܐܼܥܐܣ݁ ܐܼܡܐܢ‑ܝܣ܉ ܠܐ ܬܹܢ‑ܝܹܬ݁ܥܐܣ݁ܐ ܢܝܬܢܝ: ܡܝ ܪܹܦ̰ܕܹܢ ܐܲܨ̰ܐܪ܃ ܐܼܣܹܪܣ ܐܲܨ̰ܐܪ.

ܐܲܣܡܝ ܐܼ ܬܫܹܬܟܐ ܬܝܠܹܦ̰ܬ ܐܼ ܝܝܙܹܡ܃ ܐܼܘܐܠܐ‑ܬܹܢ. ܝܹܩ݁ܝܡ‑ܐܣ ܐܼ ܬܝܠܹܦ̰ܬ ܕܹܓ ܘܹܒܪܝܕ܃ ܡܝ ܕ‑ܬܘܥ̰ܐܠ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܐܲ ܡ݁ ܐܿܚ̰ܹܢܦ̰ܘܦ̰܃ ܐܲ ܡ݁ ܐܿܙܹܢܦ̰ܘܦ̰܃ ܕ ܐܲܫܘ ܐܼ ܡ‑ܕ‑ܝܹܢ݁ܐ ܠܡܝܪ ܢ ܠܹܘܚܘܫ܉
ܬܹܪܓܹܡ‑ܝܬ܃ ܬܹܕܥܐ‑ܝܐܣ܄ ܐܲܪܡܝ ܬܹܥܝܐ܃ ܬܹܚܟܐ‑ܝܐܣ. ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܣܝ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ:
— ܐܲܕ ܟܹܡ‑ܡܹܢܥܹܥ̰ ܣܝ ܠܡܘܬ܃ ܐܲܕ ܢܹܡܚ̰ܐܠܐܨ. ܐܲ ܬܐܡܹܗܒܘܠܬ܃ ܐܲ ܬܐܡܹܗܒܘܠܬ! ܐܼܡܝ ܐܲܪܐ ܕ ܐܲܣ‑ܬܹܟܦ̰ܹܨ̰ ܐܲܩܹܪ݁ܘ‑ܡ ܐܲܕ ܬ‑ܝܥ̰ܹܛ̰݁܃ ܣܘܐܝܹܣ ܐܲܪܐ ܬܹܛ̰ܕܹܨ̰ ܐܼܒܐܘܹܢ‑ܝܣ ܣ ܐܲܢܹܒܕܘ܉

ܬܹܩ݁ܝܡ ܬܝܠܹܦ̰ܬ ܐܲܝܹܢ ܬܹܩ݁ܝܡ܃ ܬܹܒܪܹܢ ܣ ܐܼܙܹܡ ܐܼܘܐܟܹ݁ܢ ܐܿܪ ܬܹܬ݁ܪܘܛ̰ܘ ܐܲܪܐ ܠܹܥܗܘܕ ܢ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ. ܬܹܣ݁ܐܘܹܠ‑ܐܣ܃ ܬܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܐܲ ܠܡܝܪ ܢ ܠܹܘܚܘܫ܃ ܐܿܠܐܫ ܣܝ ܪ݁ܐܝ‑ܢ݁ܝ ܐܼ ܕ‑ܢܓܹܪ!
ܝܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ‑ܕ ܐܲܘܐܠ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܐܲ ܝܹܠ݁ܝ܃ ܩܹܪܹ݁ܒ‑ܕ: ܬܘܪܐ ܘܹܣ݁ܪܹܥ̰: ܝܹܢܩܹܣ ܝܹܛ̰ܪܝ‑ܘ܃ ܝܹܪܢܐ ܐܲܣܹܠ݁ܝ‑ܘ…
ܬܟܘܟܪܐ܃ ܬܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܡܝ ܐܲܪܐ ܕ ܐܲܟ‑ܦ̰ܟܹܥ̰ ܐܲܩܹܪ݁ܘ‑ܘ ܐܲܕ ܬ‑ܬܥ̰ܹܛ̰ܹ݁ܨ̰܃ ܣܘܐܝܹܣ ܐܲܪܐ ܛ̰ܕܹܥ̰ ܐܼܒܐܘܹܢ‑ܝܟ ܣ ܐܲܢܹܒܕܘ܉
ܐܼܪܥܹܕ ܐܲܡ ܬܹܓܢܹܘܬ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܬܹܡܹ݁ܓ݁ܪܹܨ̰ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ!
— ܬܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ: ܡܹ݁ܓ݁ܪܹܥ̰‑ܬ!
ܬܹܪܘܹܠ.

Translation.Title: The Wolf, the Sow, and the Lion
Paragraphs: The wolf, knowing what he had done to both the lion and the sow, was now afraid of his own shadow. How was he to protect himself? He kept a constant eye on them: whenever they lifted a foot, he set down his foot.

When the sow went to complain to the lion, he watched them. He waited for the sow along her path, and when she was returning, he said to her:
— O snout‑mouth, O muzzle‑snout, what did the king of the animals say to you?
She insulted him and cursed him; when she grew tired, she narrated to him. Sir Mḥemmed said to her:
— I will save you from death, and we shall be even. O foolish woman, O foolish woman! Once you have given him your head to chew on, with what will you grind his broad beans in the summer?

The sow waited for a time, then she returned to the lion so as not to break her covenant with God. She called out to him and said:
— O king of the animals, nothing will come of that matter we brought up!
He answered her, saying:
— My daughter, come closer: I have grown old now: my sight has dimmed, and my hearing as well…
She hesitated and said to him:
— If I give you my head to chew on, with what will I grind your broad beans in the summer?
He roared like a thunderstorm and said to her:
— You have crossed paths with Mḥemmed!
— She replied to him: I have crossed paths with him!
And she fled.

Source.Title: ܐܼܙܹܡ ܕ ܘܹܠܥ̰ܹܡ
Paragraphs:
ܝܝܘ݁ܐܣ݁܃ ܐܼܪܘܹܠ‑ܕ ܝܝܙܹܡ: ܬܹܒܥܹܢ‑ܬ‑ܝܕ ܐܼܨܹܓ݁ܐܕܹܢ.
ܝܹܡܠܐܠ‑ܕ ܘܹܠܥ̰ܹܡ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܕܥܐܥ̰‑ܟ ܣ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ܃ ܡܐ ܐܿܪ ܐܼܝܝ‑ܬܣܹܠ݁ܟܹܨ̰܃ ܕܝ ܠܹܥܢܐܝܐ‑ܟ!
ܝܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܬ ܘܹܠܥ̰ܹܡ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܬܹܥ̰ܪܐܪܬ܃ ܐܼܥܹܒ݁ܐ‑ܬ܃ ܝܹܘ݁ܝ‑ܬ.

ܕܹܓ ܘܹܒܪܝܕ܃ ܝܹܡܠܐܠ‑ܕ ܕ ܐܼܨܹܓ݁ܐܕܹܢ܃ ܢ݁ܐܢ‑ܐܣ:
— ܐܲܝ ܐܲܠܥ̰ܹܡ܃ ܐܿܪ ܬܹܡܹ݁ܓ݁ܪܹܨ̰ ܐܲܪܐ ܐܼܙܹܡ ܐܼܥܹܕ݁ܐ܉
— ܝܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣܹܢ: ܐܼܥܹܕ݁ܐ!
ܪܘܚܹܢ܃ ܝܹܘ݁ܝ‑ܬ ܘܹܠܥ̰ܹܡ ܐܲܪܡܝ ܐܼ ܬ‑ܝܹܣ݁ܐܘܹܨ̰ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܠܹܡܢܹܥ܃ ܐܼܣܹܪܣ‑ܝܬ. ܐܼܡܝܪܹܢ ܐܼܒܓܹܣ‑ܕ ܥ̰ܘܪ‑ܣ ܝܝܙܹܡ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܐܲܕ ܟ‑ܫ̰ܹ݁ܥ̰!
— ܝܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܘܹܠܥ̰ܹܡ: ܕ ܠܡܘܚܐܠ ܐܲܝ ܕ‑ܬܨ̰ܹܠܒܹܨ̰! ܬܹܒܥܹܢ‑ܟ‑ܝܕ ܐܼܨܹܓ݁ܐܕܹܢ ܐܲܕ ܟ‑ܢܥ̰ܹܢ܃ ܣܹܠ݁ܟܹܥ̰‑ܟ ܣܝ ܠܡܘܬ: ܬܘܪܐ ܐܲܕ ܐܼܝܝ‑ܬܹܫ̰ܹ݁ܨ̰܉
ܚ̰ܹܕܡܹܥ̰‑ܐܟ ܠܚ̰ܝܪ: ܐܹܪ݁‑ܝܝܝ‑ܬ.
— ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܝܝܙܹܡ: ܐܲܕ ܟ‑ܫ̰ܹ݁ܥ̰܃ ܐܲܥܠܐܚ̰ܐܛܹܪ ܠܚ̰ܝܪ ܐܿܪ ܝܹܬ݁ܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܐܲܪܐ.
ܝܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܘܹܠܥ̰ܹܡ:
— ܕܥܐܥ̰‑ܟ ܣ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ܃ ܡܐ ܐܿܪ ܐܼܝܝ‑ܬܘܢܝܦ̰ܹܨ̰ ܐܲܕ ܪܘܚܹܥ̰ ܐܲܕ ܕ‑ܣܬܹܩܣܝܥ̰!
ܫܘܒܟܹܥ̰‑ܟ ܣ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ܃ ܡܐ ܐܿܦ̰ܝܥ̰ ܐܿܪ ܝܹܬ݁ܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܐܲܪܐ ܠܚ̰ܝܪ܃ ܐܲܪܕ ܐܲ ܕ‑ܒܹܪܢܹܥ̰ ܐܲܕ ܐܼܝܝ‑ܬܹܫ̰ܹ݁ܨ̰!
ܝܘܢܹܦ̰‑ܐܣ ܐܼܪܘܚ.

ܐܼܪܘܚ ܘܹܠܥ̰ܹܡ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܠܹܘܚܘܫ. ܐܲ ܘܝܢ ܝܹܡܹ݁ܓܹ݁ܪ܃ ܝܹܚܟܘ‑ܝܐܣ: ܝܝܘܹܢ ܐܼ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ ܐܿܪ ܐܲܣ‑ܝܹܦ̰ܟܝ ܠܚܹܩ. ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܘܹܥ̰ܝܘܠ:
— ܐܿܪ ܟ‑ܝܹܨ̰ܠܝܡ ܐܲܪܐ ܝܝܙܹܡ: ܢܹܟ݁ ܕ ܐܲܟܠܝ ܢ ܘܹܚ̰݁ܐܡ: ܐܲܕ ܥܹܒ݁ܝܥ̰܃ ܣܪܹܟܒܹܥ̰܄ ܐܲܕ ܫ̰ܹ݁ܥ̰ ܝܝܪ ܬܡܹܫܚܐ܃ ܐܲܕ ܪܢܘܥ̰ ܐܲܥܹܟ݁ܐܙ܄ ܝܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܝܝܣܹܡ‑ܝܘ ܕ ܬܐܣܹܠܩܘܒܬ: ܠܚ̰ܝܪ ܐܿܪ ܝܹܬ݁ܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܐܲܪܐ.
— ܬܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܬܝܚ̰ܣܝ: ܐܿܪ ܟ‑ܝܹܨ̰ܠܝܡ ܐܲܪܐ ܝܝܙܹܡ: ܐܲܕ ܦ̰ܟܹܥ̰ ܐܲܝܹܦ̰ܟܝ ܕ ܬܐܕܘܛ܃ ܐܲܕ ܕ‑ܐܪܘܹܥ̰ ܐܼܙܐܡܐܪܹܢ܃ ܐܲܕ ܬܹܢ‑ܙܠܘܢ܃ ܙܠܘܢ‑ܝܝܝ܄ ܫ̰ܹ݁ܢ‑ܬܹܢ܃ ܫ̰ܹ݁ܢ‑ܝܝܝ: ܠܚ̰ܝܪ ܐܿܪ ܝܹܬ݁ܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܐܲܪܐ.
— ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܘܹܙܓܹܪ: ܕ ܟܹܫ̰݁ ܐܲܝ ܕ ܨ̰݁ܐܠܹܡ: ܐܲܕ ܟܹܪܙܹܥ̰ ܐܼܪܕܹܢ ܕ ܬܹܡܛ̰ܝܢ܃ ܐܲܕ ܡܹܓ݁ܠܹܥ̰ ܐܼܙܹܡܪܐܢ ܕ ܘܘܪܬܐܢ: ܐܲܫܘ ܢ ܠܚ̰ܝܪ ܐܲܪܐ ܕ ܐܼܝܝ‑ܪܹ݁ܢ܉ ܐܲܕ ܐܼܝܝ‑ܩܹܕ݁ܡܹܢ ܣ ܐܲܥܪܝܫ! ܠܘܟܐܢ ܝܹܬ݁ܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܠܚ̰ܝܪ܃ ܬܐܠ݁ܝ ܝܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܐܼ ܘܹܙܓܹܪ.

ܝܹܒܪܹܢ ܘܹܠܥ̰ܹܡ ܕܹܓ ܐܿܥ̰ܝܠܝܦ̰ ܡܹܩܹ݁ܪ: ܡܐܫ̰݁ܝ ܐܲܟܹ݁ܢ ܝܹܒܢܐ ܐܼ‑ܝܘܦ̰ܐ: ܐܼܡܝ ܠܚ̰ܝܪ ܝܹܬ݁ܡܹܫ̰݁ܐ܃ ܐܲܕ ܐܲܣ‑ܬ‑ܝܹܫ̰݁ ܟܐܢ ܝܝܙܹܡ܃ ܝܹܫ̰݁‑ܝܬ ܙܕܹܦ̰݁ܝܪ‑ܣ.
ܠܐ ܐܼܠܹܚ݁ܘ ܘܹܠܥ̰ܹܡ ܝܹܬ݁ܪܘ: ܡܐܫ̰݁ܝ ܐܲܟܹ݁ܢ ܝܹܛܹ݁ܣ ܐܼ ܕ‑ܝܘܟܝ!

ܝܹܡܠܐܠ‑ܕ ܕ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܕܹܓ ܘܹܒܪܝܕ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ‑ܕ:
— ܕ ܐܲܫܘ ܟ‑ܝܘܥ̰ܹܢ܃ ܐܲ ܥܹܡ݁ܝ ܒܘܡܓܹܪܨ̰܉
ܝܹܚܟܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܘܹܠܥ̰ܹܡ ܬܐܡܣܐܠܬ. ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ:
— ܕ ܨܹ݁ܚ: ܠܚ̰ܝܪ ܐܿܪ ܝܹܬ݁ܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܐܲܪܐ: ܬܘܪܐ ܐܲܕ ܟ‑ܝܹܫ̰݁܃ ܐܲܝ ܐܲܡܫܘܡ.

ܝܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܘܹܠܥ̰ܹܡ ܐܲܪ ܝܹܬ݁ܪܹܥܪܹܥ. ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ:
— ܬܹܬ݁ܐܠܐܣܹܨ̰‑ܝܝܝ‑ܬ݁: ܐܲܕ ܟ‑ܣܹܠ݁ܟܹܥ̰܃ ܡܐ ܐܼܣܹܠܹ݁ܟ‑ܝܟ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ܃ ܐܲܕ ܢܹܡܚ̰ܐܠܐܨ. ܐܼܡܝܪܹܢ܃ ܝܹܡܠܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܕܹܓ ܐܿܡܹܛ̰݁ܘܥ̰.

ܐܼܪܘܚ ܘܹܠܥ̰ܹܡ ܐܲܪܡܝ ܝܹܘܹ݁ܨ̰ ܣ ܐܼܙܹܡ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܐܲ ܠܡܝܪ ܢ ܠܹܘܚܘܫ܃ ܕ ܨܹ݁ܚ: ܠܚ̰ܝܪ ܐܿܪ ܝܹܬ݁ܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܐܲܪܐ.
ܝܹܒܕܐ ܝܝܙܹܡ ܐܲܪ ܝܹܬ݁ܡܝܛ̰݁ܝܕ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܐܼܗܝ܃ ܐܲܕ ܟ‑ܫ̰ܹ݁ܥ̰!
— ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܘܹܠܥ̰ܹܡ: ܣ ܠܹܥܩܹܠ܃ ܐܲ ܠܡܝܪ ܢ ܠܹܘܚܘܫ! ܣ݁ܝܘܹܨ̰‑ܝܝܝ ܕܹܓ ܘܐܘܐܠ: ܠܚ̰ܝܪ ܐܿܪ ܝܹܬ݁ܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܐܲܪܐ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܝܝܪ ܠܐܨܹܠ: ܥ̰ܹܪ ܬܐܪ݁ܐܘܬ ܢ ܠܐܨܹܠ܃ ܠܚ̰ܝܪ ܝܹܬ݁ܘܥ̰ܐܠ.

ܝܹܕ݁ܘܩܹ݁ܣ ܝܝܙܹܡ܃ ܐܼܪܥܹܕ ܐܲܡ ܬܹܓܢܹܘܬ: ܐܿܪ ܝܹܙܡܝܪ ܐܲܪܐ ܐܲܕ ܝܹܣܹ݁ܡܣܘ ܠܐܨܹܠ‑ܝܣ. ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܐܼ ܘܹܠܥ̰ܹܡ:
— ܬܹܡܹ݁ܓ݁ܪܹܨ̰ ܐܿܫܹ݁ܢ!
— ܝܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ: ܡ݁ܘܓܪܹܥ̰‑ܬ܃ ܐܲ ܠܡܝܪ ܢ ܠܹܘܚܘܫ.
— ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܝܝܙܹܡ: ܪܘܚ: ܐܼܣܹܠܹ݁ܟ‑ܝܟ ܒܘ ܡܹܝ݁ܐ ܬܚܝܠܐ!
ܐܼܪܘܚ ܘܹܠܥ̰ܹܡ ܕܝ ܠܐܡܐܢ ܐܿ ܨ̰ܡܐܢ.

Translation.Title: The Lion and the Camel
Paragraphs:
One day, the lion fled: hunters were pursuing him. He crossed paths with the camel and said to him:
— I implore you by God, if you would only save me, under your protection!
The camel put him into a large sack, loaded him up, and carried him away.

Along the way, he met the hunters, who asked him:
— O camel, did you not cross paths with the lion passing by?
— He replied to them: He passed!
They went on. The camel carried him until he brought him to safety, and he set him down. Right then, the lion stepped up to him and said:
— I am going to eat you!
— The camel replied to him: It is an impossible thing that you demand! Hunters were pursuing you to kill you, and I saved you from death: now you want to eat me? I did a good deed for you: return it to me.
— The lion told him: I will eat you, because a good deed is never returned.
The camel replied to him:
— I implore you by God, if you would only let me go and ask! I bind you by God, if I find that a good deed is not returned, I will come back so you can eat me!
He let him go, and he departed.

The camel went to the animals. Whomever he crossed paths with, he narrated to him; not a single one, for God's sake, gave him justice. The donkey said to him:
— The lion has not wronged you: I am the slave of the house. I carry loads, I carry riders; I eat bad food, and I receive the stick besides. Then my name becomes an insult: a good deed is never returned.
— The ewe said to him: The lion has not wronged you: I give milk and wool, I bring forth lambs, they slaughter them, and they slaughter me; they eat them, and they eat me: a good deed is never returned.
— The ox said to him: It is you who are the wrongdoer: I plow the wheat and the barley, I cultivate the olive trees and the orchards: what good deed do they return to me? They lead me straight to the butchery slab! If a good deed were ever returned, it would have been returned to the ox.

The camel turned in deep sorrow; it was not as he had imagined. For since a good deed is eaten, the lion will eat it, and will eat him next.
The camel walked along weeping: it was not as he had slept that he awoke!

He crossed paths with the wolf along the way, who said to him:
— What is the matter with you, Uncle Long‑Neck?
The camel narrated the matter to him. The wolf said to him:
— It is the truth: a good deed is never returned. Now he will eat you, you wretched one.

Then the camel began to groan. The wolf said to him:
— You have a claim on me: I will save you, if God saves you, and we shall be even. Right then, he whispered into his ear.

The camel walked on until he reached the lion, and he said to him:
— O king of the animals, it is the truth: a good deed is never returned.
The lion began to stretch himself and said to him:
— Therefore, I will eat you!
The camel said to him: Gently, O king of the animals! Let me finish my words: a good deed is never returned to a wicked origin; to the children of noble origin, a good deed is always returned.

The lion startled. He roared like a thunderstorm: he could not allow his own origin to be defiled. He said to the camel:
— You have crossed paths with the wolf!
— He replied to him: I have crossed paths with him, O king of the animals.
— The lion said to him: Go; the one of a hundred ruses has saved you!
The camel departed in safety and security.

Source.Title: ܬܠܐܬܐ ܝܹܙܓܐܪܹܢ܃ ܕ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܕ ܝܝܙܹܡ
Paragraphs: ܠ݁ܐܢ ܬܠܐܬܐ ܝܹܙܓܐܪܹܢ܃ ܝܝܘܹܢ ܕ ܐܲܡܹܠ݁ܐܠ܃ ܘܐܝܹܨ̰ ܕ ܐܲܒܹܪܟܐܢ܃ ܘܝܣ ܬܠܐܬܐ ܕ ܐܲܙܹܓ݁ܐܥ̰܃ ܘܹܩܡܹܢ ܬܐܓܡܐܬ݁ ܕܝ ܬܹܛ̰ܓܝ. ܡܝ ܟܣܐܢ ܙ̰ܡܝܥ ܐܲܪ ܬܐܡܹܕ݁ܝܬ܃ ܐܲܕ ܣܹ݁ܡܠܝܠܹܢ ܬܝܣܹܨ̰ܘܐ‑ܢܣܹܢ܃ ܐܲܕ ܡܹܟ݁ܢܹܢ ܐܲܫ݁ܝܘܹܢ‑ܢܣܹܢ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܒܹܪ݁ܐ܃ ܐܲܕ ܛ݁ܣܹܢ. ܡܝ ܕ‑ܝܘܣܐ ܝܝܙܹܡ܃ ܐܲܕ ܕ‑ܝܐܦ̰ ܡܟܘܠ ܝܝܘܹܢ ܣܹܓ‑ܣܹܢ ܐܼܩܘܪܥ‑ܕ ܠܓ̰ܝܗܐ‑ܣ: ܐܲܕ ܐܲܣܹܢ‑ܕ‑ܝܹܢܹ݁ܨ̰܃ ܐܲܕ ܐܼܪܘܚ: ܐܿܪ ܐܲܣܹܢ‑ܝܹܙܡܝܪ ܐܲܪܐ.

ܝܝܘ݁ܐܣ݁܃ ܐܼܪܘܚ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܣ ܐܲܙܓܹܪ ܐܲܒܹܪܟܐܢ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܣܠܝܥ̰ ܐܼ ܘܐܬܡܐܬܹܢ‑ܝܟ ܠܐ ܬ݁ܣܹܘ݁ܝܩܹܢ ܕܹܓ‑ܟ܃ ܐܲܕ ܟ‑ܣܹܒ݁ܠܹܢ ܐܼ ܝܝܙܹܡ ܐܲܕ ܟ‑ܝܹܫ̰݁܃ ܐܲܕ ܐܲܣܹܢ‑ܕ‑ܬܹܩ݁ܝܡ ܠܥ̰ܐܒܐ ܘܹܚܕ‑ܣܹܢ.
ܐܼܥܐܘܹܕ‑ܐܣ ܐܲܟܹ݁ܢ݁ܝ ܐܼ ܘܹܙܓܹܪ ܐܲܙܹܓ݁ܐܥ̰܃ ܝܹܪܢܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܐܲܟܹ݁ܢ݁ܝ ܐܼ ܘܹܙܓܹܪ ܐܲܡܹܠ݁ܐܠ: ܝܹܨ̰ܡܹܥ ܐܲܕ ܬܹܢ‑ܝܹܣܹ݁ܡܢܹܥ̰܃ ܐܲܕ ܝܹܫ̰݁ ܣܹܓ‑ܣܹܢ.

ܝܹܣܹ݁ܟܫܹܡ‑ܐܣܹܢ ܫܹ݁ܟ݁: ܝܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܝܹܟܦ̰ܐ ܠܐܡܐܢ ܓܐܪ‑ܐܣܹܢ: ܠܐ ܬܹ݁ܡܝܹܚ̰ܛ̰ܐܪܹܢ܃ ܬܹ݁ܡܝܹܢܦ̰ܐܣܹܢ. ܡܝ ܕ‑ܝܹܘܹ݁ܨ̰ ܝܝܨ̰܃ ܕܝ ܠܥܘܨ̰ ܐܲܪܐ ܣܹ݁ܡܠܝܠܹܢ ܬܝܣܹܨ̰ܘܐ‑ܢܣܹܢ ܐܲܡ ܙܝܟ܃ ܡܹܟ݁ܢܹܢ ܐܲܫ݁ܝܘܹܢ‑ܢܣܹܢ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܒܹܪ݁ܐ܃ ܐܿܥ̰ܐܠܹܢ ܠܐ ܣܹ݁ܡܠܝܠܹܢ ܐܲܫ݁ܝܘܹܢ‑ܢܣܹܢ܃ ܬܹ݁ܡܥܐܣ݁ܐܢ ܢ ܘܐܝ ܓܐܪ‑ܐܣܹܢ.

ܝܝܘ݁ܐܣ݁܃ ܝܹܘܬ‑ܕ ܝܝܙܹܡ ܐܲܙܓܹܪ ܐܲܒܹܪܟܐܢ܃ ܝܹܪܛ̰ܐ‑ܬ ܕܝ ܬܩܹܨܪܝܬ܃ ܝܹܘ݁ܝ‑ܬ܃ ܝܹܫ̰݁ܐ‑ܬ. ܐܲܣ݁ ܢ݁ܝܨ̰ܹܢ܃ ܝܹܘܬ‑ܕ ܐܲܙܓܹܪ ܐܲܙܹܓ݁ܐܥ̰܃ ܝܹܪܛ̰ܐ‑ܬ ܕܝ ܬܩܹܨܪܝܬ܃ ܝܹܘ݁ܝ‑ܬ܃ ܝܹܫ̰݁ܐ‑ܬ. ܝܹܩ݁ܝܡ‑ܕ ܘܹܙܓܹܪ ܐܲܡܹܠ݁ܐܠ ܘܹܚܕ‑ܣ܃ ܐܲܡ ܓܘܙ̰ܝܠ: ܐܹܘܬ‑ܝܬ܃ ܐܼ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ: ܐܹܓ̰݁‑ܝܬ܃ ܐܼ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ!

ܝܹܩ݁ܝܡ‑ܕ ܘܹܙܓܹܪ ܐܲܡܹܠ݁ܐܠ ܠܐ ܝܹܬ݁ܪܘ ܦ̰ ܘܐܬܡܐܬܹܢ‑ܝܣ܃ ܝܹܬܹ݁ܪܓܝܓܝ ܦ̰ ܝܝܡܐܢ‑ܝܣ. ܐܼܪܘܚ ܣ ܐܿܫܹ݁ܢ ܐܲܕ ܬ‑ܝܕ‑ܝܫܝܘܹܪ. ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܕܥܐܥ̰‑ܟ ܣ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ: ܨ̰ܹܒܹ݁ܪ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܝ ܐܲܟܹ݁ܢ ܬܨ̰ܹܒ݁ܪܹܨ̰ ܦ̰ ܘܹܠܥ̰ܹܡ ܕ ܬܝܠܹܦ̰ܬ܃ ܡܐ ܐܿܠܐܫ ܐܲܕ ܐܼܝܝ‑ܝܹܫ̰݁ ܝܝܙܹܡ!
ܐܼܗܘܙ ܐܲܩܹܪ݁ܘ‑ܣ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ܃ ܝܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ‑ܕ:
— ܕܹ݁ܥܘܐ‑ܟ ܬܹܘܥܹܪ!
ܝܹܥܪܹܨ̰ ܒܘ ܡܹܝ݁ܐ ܬܚܝܠܐ ܐܲ ܣ‑ܝܹܣܹ݁ܦ̰ܗܹܡ ܬܐܡܣܐܠܬ: ܐܲܙܓܹܪ܃ ܢܹ݁ܝ݁ܐ‑ܣ ܕ ܬܐܙܘܪܐܢܬ: ܐܿܪ ܐܲܣ‑ܝܘܦ̰ܝ ܐܲܪܐ ܐܲܡܹܟ ܐܲܪܐ ܬ‑ܝܹܣܥ̰ܹܪ. ܝܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܐܼܥܹܓܹ݁ܢ‑ܐܣ:
— ܐܲܣܡܝ ܬܹܡܹ݁ܓ݁ܪܹܨ̰ ܠܡܝܪ ܢ ܠܹܘܚܘܫ܃ ܣܝܘܹܠ‑ܐܣ ܬܝܕܹܬ݁.

ܝܝܘ݁ܐܣ݁ ܕܹܓ ܘܘܣ݁ܐܢ ܓܹܪ ܐܿܢܹܒܕܘ ܕ ܬܹܦ̰ܣܘܬ܃ ܕ݁ܘܢܝܬ ܬܹܙܹ݁ܓܙܹܘ ܬܹܓ̰݁ܘܓ̰ܹ݁ܓ܃ ܛܝܟ݁ܘܟ ܠܐ ܝܹܟ݁ܐܬ܃ ܝܹܘܬ‑ܕ ܢ݁ܐܥܘܪ ܐܲܙܓܹܪ ܐܲܡܹܠ݁ܐܠ: ܝܹܙ̰ܦ̰ܹܠ܃ ܬܐܣܹܛ݁ܐ‑ܣ ܕܹܓ ܓܹܢ݁ܝ܃ ܠܐ ܝܹܣܪܘܗܡܘܬ܃ ܐܼܪܹܓܹ݁ܠ: ܬܐܠܐܬ ܬܹܬ݁ܐܟ‑ܝܬ ܐܼ ܬܐܠܐܬ܃ ܐܼܥ̰ܛ̰ܹܪ ܐܼ ܝܹܥ̰ܛ̰ܹܪ܃ ܬܝܥ̰ܝܠܬ ܐܼ ܬܝܥ̰ܝܠܬ܃ ܐܲܪܡܝ ܝܹܥ̰ܠܝ ܦ̰ ܝܝܙܹܡ ܐܿܪ ܝܹܒܢܝ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܐܣ.
ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܕ ܐܲܫܘ ܟ‑ܝܕ‑ܝܹܘ݁ܝܢ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܕܐܓܝ܃ ܐܲ ܡ݁ܝܣ ܢ ܬܦ̰ܘܢܐܣܬ܉ ܟܪܐ ܕ݁ܐܘ ܐܿܩܹܪ݁ܘ‑ܟ! ܠܐܡܹܥܢܐ܃ ܥܘܗܕܹܥ̰‑ܟ ܣ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ ܐܿܪ ܟ‑ܫ̰݁ܝܥ̰ ܡܐ ܬܣܐܘܠܹܨ̰‑ܝܝܝ ܬܝܕܹܬ݁.
ܐܼܥ̰ܝܠ ܐܲܕ ܕ‑ܝܹܣܟܝܕܹ݁ܒ܃ ܐܲܕ ܬ‑ܝܹܫ̰݁. ܝܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܐܿܥܹܪ݁ܘܡ:
— ܐܿܚܹܩ ܘܐܕܝ… ܕ ܘܐܕܝ… ܐܲ ܠܡܝܪ ܢ ܠܹܘܚܘܫ܃ ܐܲ ܠܘܟܐܢ ܛ̰ܪܝܥ̰ ܐܲܕ ܟ‑ܝܕ‑ܐܦ̰ܹܥ̰ ܕܐܓܝ܃ ܐܿܪ ܕ‑ܪܘܝܠܹܥ̰܃ ܥ̰ܐܣ ܐܲܕ ܝܹܫ̰݁ ܢ݁ܐܥܘܪ ܬܐܣܐ‑ܘ! ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܝ ܣܝ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ: ܣܝܘܹܠ‑ܐܣ ܬܝܕܹܬ݁!
ܐܼܪܥܹܕ ܝܝܙܹܡ ܐܲܡ ܬܹܓܢܹܘܬ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ:
— ܪܘܚ! ܬܣܹܠܟܹܨ̰ ܐܲ ܒܘ ܢܹ݁ܝ݁ܐ.
ܡܐ ܐܿܪ ܬܹܣ݁ܝܢܹܨ̰ ܐܲܪܐ ܐܲܕ ܬܹܣܟܝܕ݁ܒܹܨ̰܃ ܣܝܘܹܠ ܬܝܕܹܬ݁: ܢܹ݁ܝ݁ܐ ܬܹܣܹ݁ܪܒܐܚ ܢܹܥ̰ ܬܹܣ݁ܘܟ݁ܘܣ.

Translation.Title: The Three Oxen, the Wolf, and the Lion
Paragraphs: There were three oxen: one was white, another black, and the third red; they formed a brotherhood in the forest. When they grazed together until evening, they would join their backsides together, project their horns outward, and sleep. When the lion arrived, he would find that every single one of them was guarding his own side; he would circle around them and leave, for he was not strong enough to face them.

One day, the wolf went to the black ox and said to him:
— I heard your brothers plotting against you; they are going to sacrifice you to the lion so he will eat you, and then the forest will belong to them alone.
He repeated the same thing to the red ox, and did the same again to the white ox, hoping to set them against one another so that he could eat from their remains.

He planted doubt among them, and from then on trust was finished between them: they glared at one another with hostility and mutual suspicion. When night fell, instead of joining their backsides as they used to do, projecting their horns outward, they turned to join their horns inward, watching each other for any sudden betrayal.

One day, the lion struck the black ox, broke his spine, carried him away, and ate him. Another day, he struck the red ox, broke his spine, carried him away, and ate him. The white ox was left all alone, like an orphan: strike him, for God's sake—leave him, for God's sake!

The white ox remained there weeping for his brothers and trembling for his own skin. He went to the wolf to seek his counsel. He said to him:
— I implore you by God: advise me just as you advised the camel and the sow, otherwise the lion will eat me!
The wolf shook his head and answered him:
— Your case is a difficult one!
The master of a hundred ruses tried to explain the matter to him, but the ox's innocence was too thick: the wolf found no way to instruct him. Finally, he gave him this warning:
— When you cross paths with the king of the animals, speak the truth to him.

One day during the seasons between summer and spring, when the world was green and blooming and the coucou bird was calling, the horsefly struck the white ox. He bolted in a panic, his tail raised high into the air, bellowing and running blindly: valley gave him up to valley, ravine to ravine, ridge to ridge, until he crashed right on top of the lion without having expected him.
The lion said to him:
— What has brought you here, O son of the cow? Something bad is brewing under your head! However, I covenant with you by God that I will not eat you if you tell me the truth.
The lion thought he would catch him in a lie and eat him. The honest simpleton replied to him:
— By the truth of this… and this… O king of the animals, if I had known I would find you here, I would never have fled my home, even if the horsefly had eaten my very liver! Sir Mḥemmed told me: speak the truth to him!
The lion roared like a thunderstorm and said to him:
— Go! Your innocence has saved you, O master of simplicity.
If you do not know how to lie, speak the truth: innocence brings good fortune or delivers one from ruin.

Source.Title: ܐܼܙܹܡ ܕ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܕ ܝܝܦ̰ܝܣ
Paragraphs:
ܐܲܣܡܝ ܝܘܦ̰ܐ ܝܝܙܹܡ ܐܲܢܓܐ ܬܹܢܬ‑ܝܓܹܪ ܩ݁ܘܪܹܢܬ ܣܹܓ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ܃ ܐܲܝܹܢ ܐܲܪܐ ܕ‑ܝܹܓ̰݁ ܐܲܕ ܬ‑ܝܕ‑ܝܐܦ̰ ܝܹܫ̰݁ܐ‑ܬ ܢܹܬ݁ܐ ܕ ܝܝܦ̰ܝܣ ܠܐ ܬ‑ܬ݁ܐܒܐܥܹܢ܃ ܝܹܡܨܐܠܐܚ ܝܝܕ‑ܣܹܢ ܐܼ ܣܝܢ܃ ܐܼܥܐܗܹܕ‑ܝܬܹܢ ܣ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ ܐܿܪ ܬܹܢ‑ܝܹܫ̰݁ܝ. ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܝܝܙܹܡ ܐܼ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ:
'' ܝ݁ܐ܃ ܐܲ ܕ݁ܝܒ܃ ܐܲܕ ܢܨܐܦ̰ܹܪ܃''
'' ܕ ܪ݁ܒܹܚ‑ܝܟ ܐܼܒܐܢ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܝ:''
'' ܡܐ ܢܥ̰ܝܥ̰ ܣܝ ܡܹܕܹ݁ܢ܃ ܐܲܕ ܬܹܫ̰ܹ݁ܨ̰܄''
'' ܡܐ ܢܥ̰ܐܢ‑ܝ ܡܹܕܹ݁ܢ܃ ܬܹܫ̰ܹ݁ܨ̰‑ܝ!''
ܫܹܪܟܹܢ ܬܐܚ̰ܹܪ݁ܐܛ̰ܬ ܣܹܓ ܘܐܣ݁‑ܢ݁ܝ: ܢܝܬܢܝ ܬ݁ܩܹܕ݁ܝܡܹܢ‑ܐܣ‑ܕ ܨ݁ܝܐܕܐ܄ ܢܹܬ݁ܐ ܝܹܬ݁ܥ̰ܝܡܝ‑ܝܐܣ ܕܹܓ ܘܹܡܨ̰ܝܩ܃ ܝܹܬ݁ܪܘܛ̰ܘ‑ܬ݁. ܡܝ ܝܹܟܦ̰ܐ ܠܡܐܟܠܐ܃ ܫ̰ܹ݁ܢ ܢܝܬܢܝ ܬܝܣܝܓܐܪ. ܠܚܐܢ ܐܲܟܹ݁ܢ݁ܝ ܐܲܝܹܢ ܠܚܐܢ.

ܝܝܘ݁ܐܣ݁܃ ܢܥ̰ܐܢ‑ܕ ܐܲܚ̰ܹܪܦ̰ܝ ܕ ܬܝܚ̰ܣܝ ܕ ܐܼܙܝܡܹܪ. ܐܼܨ̰ܠܹܒ‑ܕ ܝܝܦ̰ܝܣ ܒܹܛ݁ܘ. ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܝܝܙܹܡ:
— ܦ̰ܹܪܩ‑ܝܬܹܢ ܓܐܪ‑ܐܢܹܥ̰.
ܐܼܦ̰ܹܪܩ‑ܝܬܹܢ ܝܝܦ̰ܝܣ: ܐܲܚ̰ܹܪܦ̰ܝ ܐܼ ܝܝܙܹܡ܃ ܬܝܚ̰ܣܝ ܐܼ ܝܝܡܐܢ‑ܝܣ܃ ܐܼܙܝܡܹܪ ܐܼ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ. ܝܹܘܬ‑ܝܬ ܝܝܙܹܡ܃ ܢܬܐܢ ܘܐܫ݁ܐܪܹܢ‑ܝܣ ܕܝ ܬܐܣܐ‑ܣ܃ ܝܹܕ݁ܐ‑ܕ ܠܹܥܡܹܪ‑ܝܣ. ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܐܼ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ:
— ܦ̰ܹܪܩ‑ܝܬܹܢ ܟܹܫ̰݁ܝܢܝ.
— ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ: ܐܲ ܠܡܝܪ ܢ ܠܹܘܚܘܫ܃ ܐܼܙܝܡܹܪ܃ ܐܲܕ ܬܣܹܦ̰ܣܘܨ̰ ܝܹܣ݁ ܐܼܡܝ‑ܟ܄ ܐܲܚ̰ܹܪܦ̰ܝ܃ ܐܲܕ ܬܦ̰ܹܬܪܹܨ̰ ܝܹܣ݁܄ ܬܝܚ̰ܣܝ܃ ܐܲܕ ܬ݁‑ܬܹܫ̰ܹ݁ܨ̰ ܕ ܐܼܡܹܢܣܝ.
— ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܝܝܙܹܡ: ܘܝ ܟ‑ܝܹܦ̰ܟܐܢ ܬܐܡܘܣܢܝ‑ܝܐܓܝ܃ ܐܲ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ܉
— ܐܼܓ̰ܐܘܹܒ‑ܝܬ‑ܝܕ: ܕ ܐܲܫ݁ܐܪܹܢ‑ܝܟ ܝܹܢܬܐܢ ܕܝ ܬܐܣܐ ܢ ܝܝܦ̰ܝܣ!

Translation.Title: The Lion, the Wolf, and the Hyena
Paragraphs:
Once the lion realized that all his attempts against the wolf had failed, and whatever prey he left behind would be eaten by the wolf and the hyena —who both always followed him—, he then made peace with them. He covenanted with them by God that he would never eat them. The lion said to the wolf:
'' Come, O wolf, let us travel together,''
'' Your good fortune is guaranteed with me:''
'' If I kill anyone, you shall eat;''
'' If anyone kills me, you shall eat me!''

They joined together in banditry from that day forward: the two of them would flush out the prey, while he would wait for it in his place and crush it down. When he finished eating, they would eat the scraps. They went on like this for some time.

One day, they killed a ram, a ewe, and a lamb. The hyena demanded a division of the spoils. The lion said to him:
— Divide them among us.
The hyena divided them: the ram for the lion, the ewe for himself, and the lamb for the wolf. The lion struck him, his claws sinking deep into his liver, and his life went with it. Then he said to the wolf:
— You do the dividing yourself.
— The wolf said to him: O king of the animals, as for the lamb, you shall open your mouth with it; as for the ram, you shall lunch on it; and as for the ewe, you shall eat her for your dinner.
— The lion said to him: Who gave you such wisdom as this, O Mḥemmed?
— He answered him: Your claws sinking into the liver of the hyena!

Source.Title: ܐܼܙܹܡ ܕ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܕ ܐܿܣܹܪܕܘܢ
Paragraphs:
ܝܹܠܚܐ ܝܝܙܹܡ ܕ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܐܲܝܹܢ ܠܚܐܢ܃ ܡܠܐܠܹܢ‑ܕ ܕ ܐܿܣܹܪܕܘܢ.
ܥܘܗܕܹܢ‑ܬ ܣ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ ܐܿܪ ܬ‑ܫ̰݁ܝܢ܃ ܐܿܥ̰ܐܠܹܢ ܕ݁ܘܟܠܹܢ.
ܐܲܣܹܪܕܘܢ ܝܹܪܘܐ ܠܹܚܫܝܫ: ܐܼܕܹܘܹ݁ܪ܃ ܝܹܠܹ݁ܡܠܹܡ܃ ܐܲܕ ܬ‑ܬܹܕܗܹܢ ܬܝܩܝܬ ܢ ܙ݁ܝܬ.
ܡܝ ܡ݁ܘܩܠܹܢ ܕܹܓ‑ܣ ܐܼܡܹܕ݁ܘܟܐܠ‑ܝܣ܃ ܐܲܪ ܕ‑ܝܹܬ݁ܐܪܹܘ ܝܝܡܝ‑ܢܣܹܢ ܐܲܡܐܢ.

ܐܿܥ̰ܐܠܹܢ ܡܫܐܘܐܪܹܢ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܐܣ ܐܲܕ ܬ‑ܫ̰ܹ݁ܢ܃ ܪܛ̰ܹܢ ܠܹܥܗܘܕ ܢ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ. ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ:
— ܢܹܟܢܝ ܐܲܩܠ‑ܐܥ̰ ܢܹܡ݁ܘܬ ܣܝ ܠܐܛ̰: ܝܹܣܹ݁ܦ̰ܟ ܝܝܘܹܢ ܣܹܓ‑ܢܹܥ̰ ܐܲܕ ܐܼܣܹܒܹ݁ܠ ܐܼܡܐܢ‑ܝܣ ܐܼܘܐܟܹ݁ܢ ܐܲܕ ܣܹܠܟܹܢ ܘܝܝܐܨ̰! ܬܘܪܐ܃ ܐܲ ܘܝܢ ܝܹܠ݁ܐܢ ܕ ܝܝܪ ܠܐܨܹܠ ܕܹܓ‑ܢܹܥ̰܃ ܐܲܕ ܬ‑ܢܹܫ̰݁.
ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܝܝܙܹܡ:
— ܢܹܟ݁܃ ܒܐܒܐ ܕ ܐܼܙܹܡ܃ ܝܹܡ݁ܐ ܕ ܬܐܣܹܕ݁ܐ!
ܐܼܢܛܹܩ‑ܕ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ:
— ܐܿܠܐܫ ܠܐܨܹܠ ܝܝܦ̰ܹܢ ܐܲܚ̰݁ܐܡ ܢ ܠܡܝܪ ܢ ܠܹܘܚܘܫ!
ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ:
— ܢܹܟ݁܃ ܒܐܒܐ ܕ ܐܿܫܹ݁ܢ܃ ܝܹܡ݁ܐ ܕ ܬܘܫܹ݁ܢܬ.
ܐܼܢܛܹܩ‑ܕ ܝܝܙܹܡ܃ ܝܹܢ݁ܐ:
— ܕ ܠܐܨܹܠ!
ܝܹܩ݁ܝܡ‑ܕ ܐܿܣܹܪܕܘܢ: ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣܹܢ:
— ܢܹܟ݁܃ ܝܹܡ݁ܐ ܕ ܬܐܓܡܐܪܬ܃ ܚ̰ܐܠܝ ܕ ܐܲܥܘܕܝܘ܄ ܥ̰ܐܣ ܐܲܪ ܒܐܒܐ܃ ܐܿܪ ܬ‑ܣ݁ܝܢܹܥ̰ ܐܲܪܐ. (ܝܘܓܐܕ ܐܲܕ ܕ‑ܝܝܢܝ ܕ ܐܲܥ̰ܝܘܠ.)
ܢ݁ܐܢ‑ܐܣ:
— ܡܐܫ̰݁ܝ ܐܲܟ݁ܐ! ܐܼܢܝ‑ܝܐܢܹܥ̰ ܘܝ ܕ ܒܐܒܐ‑ܟ ܢܹܥ̰ ܐܲܕ ܟ‑ܢܹܫ̰݁!
— ܝܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣܹܢ‑ܕ: ܣܹܪ݁ܚܹܬ‑ܝܝܝ ܐܲܕ ܪܘܚܹܥ̰ ܐܲܕ ܕ‑ܣܬܹܩܣܝܥ̰ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܐܣ. ܫܘܒܟܹܥ̰‑ܟܹܢ ܣ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ ܐܲܪܕ ܐܲ ܕ‑ܘܥ̰ܐܠܹܥ̰܃ ܐܲܕ ܐܲܘܹܢ‑ܕ‑ܐܘܝܥ̰ ܠܹܚ̰ܒܐܪ ܢ ܨܹ݁ܚ.
ܣܹܪ݁ܚܹܢ‑ܐܣ ܐܼܪܘܚ.

Translation.Title: The Lion, the Wolf, and the Mule
Paragraphs:
The lion and the wolf walked on for some time, and they crossed paths with the mule.
They covenanted with him by God that they would not eat him, and from then on they traveled together.
The mule ate his fill of grass: he grew round and shone, as though a drop of oil had anointed him.
Whenever his companions looked at him, their mouths would water.

Eventually, they plotted against him to eat him, breaking the covenants of God. The wolf said to him:
— We are dying of hunger: one of us must sacrifice himself so that the others can survive! Therefore, whoever among us has a wicked origin, we shall eat him.
The lion said:
— As for me, my father is a lion, and my mother is a lioness!
The wolf spoke up and said:
— There is no lineage finer than the house of the king of the animals!
Then the wolf said:
— As for me, my father is a wolf, and my mother is a she‑wolf.
The lion spoke up and said:
— What a lineage!
That left only the mule, who said to them:
— As for me, my mother is a mare, and my maternal uncle is a stallion; but as for my father, I never knew him. (He was afraid to say it was a donkey.)
They said to him:
— Not so! Tell us who your father is, or else we will eat you!
— He replied to them: Allow me to go and ask about him. I bind you by God that I will return and bring you the true word.
They let him go, and he departed.

Source.Title: ܠܡܘܬ ܢ ܝܝܙܹܡ
Paragraphs: ܝܘܥ̰ܐܠ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܝܹܛܹ݁ܦ̰ ܐܲܣܹܪܕܘܢ ܘܹܚܕ‑ܣ܃ ܣܹܘ݁ܩܹܢ ܕܹܓ ܐܿܩܹܪ݁ܘ ܢ ܝܝܙܹܡ܃ ܐܲܕ ܐܼܪܘܚ ܐܲܡ ܬܐܕܠܐ ܝܹܫ̰݁ܐ ܝܝܠܹܦ̰.

ܝܹܘܹ݁ܨ̰ ܐܿܣܹܪܕܘܢ ܣ ܐܲܚܹܕ݁ܐܕ: ܐܼܓܹܪܹ݁ܙ‑ܐܣ‑ܕ ܬܐܣܡܝܪܬ܃ ܐܼܢܩܹܫ‑ܝܬ݁‑ܝܕ܃ ܝܹܣܥ̰ܹܙܦ̰‑ܐܣ‑ܕ ܐܼܡܹܣܡܐܪܹܢ܃ ܣ݁ܝܹܢ܃ ܐܼܒܪܹܢ‑ܕ ܣ ܐܼܡܹܕ݁ܘܟܐܠ‑ܝܣ. ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܝܝܙܹܡ:
— ܐܼܗܝ܃ ܐܲܢܘܐ ܐܼ ܕ ܒܐܒܐ‑ܟ܉
— ܝܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܐܿܣܹܪܕܘܢ: ܐܿܪ ܐܿܦ̰ܝܥ̰ ܐܲܪܐ ܠܹܚ̰ܒܐܪ‑ܝܣ܃ ܠܐܡܹܥܢܐ ܝܹܓ̰݁ܐ‑ܝܝ‑ܕ ܬ݁ܐܙ̰ܝܪܐ ܕܹܓ ܨ̰ܐܪܹ݁ܢ‑ܝܘ: ܡܐ ܬܹܒܥ̰ܐܡ ܐܲܕ ܬ݁‑ܝܕ‑ܬܹܥ̰ܪܹܡ.
ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܝܝܙܹܡ ܐܼ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ:
— ܩܹܪܹ݁ܒ ܐܹܥ̰ܪ‑ܝܬ݁‑ܝܕ܃ ܐܲ ܡܚܹܡܹ݁ܕ.
— ܝܹܪ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ: ܐܲ ܠܡܝܪ ܢ ܠܹܘܚܘܫ܃ ܢܹܟ݁܃ ܐܼܡܐܘܠܐܢ‑ܝܘ ܕ ܐܼܓܹܠ݁ܝܠܹܢ: ܐܿܪ ܐܼܝܝ‑ܦ̰ܟܝܢ ܥ̰ܹܪ ܠܹܩܪܐܝܐ. ܕ ܟܹܫ̰݁ ܐܲܝ ܕ ܡ݁ܝܣ ܢ ܘܹܚ̰݁ܐܡ ܐܲܡܹܩܪܐܢ: ܬܹܣܹ݁ܢܨ̰ ܐܲܕ ܬ݁‑ܝܕ‑ܬܹܥ̰ܪܹܨ̰.
ܐܼܩܹܪܹ݁ܒ ܝܝܙܹܡ ܐܲܚ̰ܹܢܫܘܫ‑ܝܣ܃ ܝܹܣܬܹܥܡܹܠ ܐܲܕ ܐܼܥ̰ܹܪ: ܠܹܥܡܐܪܐ ܬܹܪܥ̰ܐ: ܐܼܒܹܕ݁ ܐܿܣܹܪܕܘܢ ܦ̰ ܐܼܡܹܙܘܘܪܐ܃ ܝܹܘܬ‑ܝܬ‑ܝܕ ܣ ܐܼܢܹܓ݁ܘܪܐ: ܟܹܫܡܹܢ ܐܼܡܹܣܡܐܪܹܢ ܕܝ ܠܡܘܚ̰ ܢ ܝܝܙܹܡ܃ ܝܹܥ̰ܠܝ.

ܘܹܪܥܐܕ ܝܹܣ݁ܘܦ̰ܹܥ̰ ܬܐܪܘܝܚܬ܃ ܝܹܥܢܐ‑ܬ ܘܘܫܹ݁ܢ ܣ ܐܲܫܹܟ݁ܐܒ.
ܝܹܢ݁ܐ‑ܝܐܣ ܝܝܙܹܡ:
— ܐܲܗ! ܕ݁ܘܢܝܬ ܕ ܘܝ ܐܼܒܹܕܹ݁ܢ܃ ܥ̰ܐܣ ܐܲܕ ܝܝܠܝ ܒܐܒܐ‑ܣ ܕ ܐܲܥ̰ܝܘܠ!

ܝܹܡ݁ܘܬ ܝܝܙܹܡ܃ ܒܘ ܬܝܣ݁ܐܣ܃ ܠܡܝܪ ܢ ܠܹܘܚܘܫ: ܝܹܢܥ̰ܐ‑ܬ ܐܿܣܹܪܕܘܢ܃ ܡ݁ܝ‑ܣ ܢ ܘܹܥ̰ܝܘܠ܃ ܫ̰݁ܐܢ‑ܬ ܘܘܫ݁ܐܢܹܢ.
ܣܹܓ ܘܐܣ݁‑ܢ݁ܝ ܐܲܝ ܬܚ̰ܐܒ ܬܡܘܪܬ.

Translation.Title: The Death of the Lion
Paragraphs: In the meantime, the wolf took the mule aside, and they plotted against the head of the lion, so that he would go down like a bundle of straw eaten by a boar.

The mule went to a blacksmith, who fitted him with fine shoes, engraved them, and left the nails protruding long. Then, he turned back to his companions. The lion said to him:
— Well then, who is your father?
— The mule replied to him: "I could not find any word of him, but he left me an inscription under my hooves; if you wish, you may read it.
The lion said to the wolf:
— Come closer and read it, O Mḥemmed.
— The wolf replied to him: O king of the animals, as for me, my parents were poor folk: they never sent me to school. It is you who are the child of a great house; you know how to read it.

The lion brought his snout close, feigning an ability to read: the charge was primed. The mule planted himself on his front legs and struck out with his hind ones; the nails entered straight into the brain of the lion, and he fell.

Before he had even given up his soul, the wolf was already at his hock, biting him.
The lion said to him:
— Ah! The world belongs to whoever stands strong, even if his father is a donkey!

Thus died the lion, the master of courage, the king of the animals: he was killed by the mule, the son of a donkey, and the wolves ate him.
It is from that very day that the land fell into ruin.

Source.Title: ܐܼ ܘܐܪ݁ܐܫ
Paragraphs:
ܬܐܡܐܫܐܗܘܬ‑ܝܘ ܠܘܐܕ ܠܘܐܕ:
ܣܐܘܠܹܥ̰‑ܬ݁‑ܝܕ ܐܼ ܬܐܪ݁ܐܘܬ ܢ ܠܹܓ̰ܘܐܕ.
ܢܹܟܢܝ ܢܪܘܚ ܐܲܒܪܝܕ ܐܲܒܪܝܕ܃
ܐܿܫܹ݁ܢ ܐܼܪܘܚ ܠܹܚ̰ܠܐ ܠܹܚ̰ܠܐ:
ܝܹܘܬ‑ܐܥ̰‑ܕ ܣ ܬܹܣܦ̰ܹܢܓ̰ܹܬ݁: ܢܹܫ̰݁ܐ‑ܬ݁܄
ܢܹܘܬ‑ܝܬ ܣ ܘܹܛ̰ܪܘ܃ ܢܹܪܛ̰ܐ‑ܬ!
ܢܹܟܢܝ܃ ܐܲܕ ܐܲܥ̰‑ܝܹܪܚܹܡ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ܄
ܐܿܫ݁ܐܢܹܢ܃ ܐܲܕ ܬܹܢ‑ܝܹܚܪܹܩ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ!

ܬܐܣܹܟ݁ܘܪܬ ܬܹܙܪܹܥ ܬܝܢܹܩ݁ܝܫܬ܃
ܬܹܦ̰ܟܐ‑ܕ ܐܼܙ̰ܹܓ̰݁ܝܓܹܢ:
ܬܹܓܠܐܠܹܙ ܕܹܓ‑ܣ܃
ܬܹܠܣܐ‑ܕ ܐܲܡ ܬܹܣܠܝܬ.
ܬܹܡ݁ܘܩܹܠ ܣ ܐܼܓܹܢ݁ܝ܃
ܬܟܹܚܹ݁ܠ‑ܕ ܛܝܛ݁ܘܫܬ‑ܝܣ
ܬܹܙܓܹܪ ܬܝܥ̰ܛ̰ܹܪܬ܃
ܬܹܩܹ݁ܢ‑ܕ ܠܚܹܢ݁ܝ.
ܬܨܘܒ݁ ܬܐܟܹܣ݁ܐܪܬ܃
ܬܹܪܟܹܒ ܦ̰ ܬܣܹܪܕܘܢܬ‑ܝܣ.

ܐܿܫܹ݁ܢ ܝܹܙܪܹܥ ܬܝܢܹܩ݁ܝܫܬ܃
ܬܹܦ̰ܟܐ‑ܕ ܐܼܣܹܢ݁ܐܢܹܢ:
ܝܹܓܠܐܠܹܙ ܕܹܓ‑ܣ܃
ܬܹܕ݁ܐ‑ܕ ܬܹܒܨ̰ܐܢܬ‑ܝܣ.
ܝܹܡ݁ܘܩܹܠ ܣ ܐܼܓܹܢ݁ܝ܃
ܬܹܕܹ݁ܪܥ̰ܹܠ ܬܛܝܛ݁ܘܫܬ‑ܝܣ.
ܝܹܙܓܹܪ ܬܝܥ̰ܛ̰ܹܪܬ܃
ܬܹܕ݁ܐ‑ܕ ܬܡܹܣ݁ܐܛ‑ܝܣ.
ܝܘܠܝ‑ܕ ܬܐܣܐܘܹܢܬ܃
ܬܹܪܨ̰‑ܕ ܬܛ̰ܹܡ݁ܘܡܬ‑ܝܣ.

Translation.Title: To the Children
Paragraphs:
My story goes along the river, along the river:
I have recited it for the children of noble souls.
We went along the path, along the path,
While the wolf took to the wild, to the wild:
He threw a fritter to us, and we ate it;
We threw a stone at him, and we broke him!
As for us, may God have mercy on us;
As for the wolves, may God burn them!

The partridge sowed a small plot,
And it brought forth flowers:
She rolled and tumbled in it,
And she was dressed like a bride.
She looked up toward the sky,
And it painted her sweet eye with kohl.
She crossed the mountain stream,
And it bound her feet with henna.
She went down the slope,
Riding upon her mule.

The wolf sowed a small plot,
And it brought forth thorns:
He rolled and tumbled in it,
And his skin was torn away.
He looked up toward the sky,
And his sweet eye was blinded.
He crossed the mountain stream,
And his thigh was carried away.
He went up the steep slope,
And his snout burst open.

Source.Title: ܠܚ̰ܐܬ݁ܝܡܐ
Paragraphs:
ܐܲ ܘܝܕܹܢ ܐܼܪܟܹܠ ܐܼ ܝܝ‑ܕ‑ܝܹܣܠܐܢ܃
ܐܿܪ ܢܹܠ݁ܝ ܕ ܐܼܡܘܢܐܢ܃
ܐܲܕ ܬܡܹܝ݁ܙܹܡ ܬܐܚܟܐܝܬ‑ܐܓܝ.
ܕ ܟܹܢܘܝ ܝܐܟ݁ ܐܲܝ ܕ‑ܠܗܐܥ̰܃
ܐܼܘܐܟܹ݁ܢ ܐܲܕ ܟܹܢ‑ܡܹܢܥܹܥ̰܃
ܣܝ ܬܝܝܬܘܝܢ ܢ ܪܹܒ݁ܝ.

ܐܲ ܘܝܢ ܝܹܠ݁ܐܢ ܕܝ ܠܚܹܟܡܐ
ܝܹܚ̰ܕܹܡ ܠܹܘܩܐܡܐ܃
ܒܐܫ ܐܲܕ ܝܹܪܟܹܒ܃ ܐܿܪ ܝܹܬ݁ܪܘܣ.
ܐܲܕ ܝܹܦ̰ܟ ܠܹܩܕܹܪ ܐܼ ܐܿܡܹܩܪܐܢ܃
ܐܼܚܐܕܹܪ ܐܲܡܹܛ̰ܝܐܢ܃
ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܐܣ ܐܿܪ ܬ݁ܐܟܹܢ ܐܲܦ̰ܘܣ.

ܐܼܙܹܡ܃ ܝܹܠ݁ܐ ܕܹܓ ܘܐܘܐܠ܃
ܐܼܙܹܡܪܹܢ ܐܼ ܫ݁ܘܐܠ܃
ܣܹ݁ܡܪܐܪܥ̰ܹܢ‑ܬ ܕܹܓ ܘܹܡܪܐܚ.
ܚ̰ܹܠ݁ܝ ܥܐܕ ܐܲ ܒܘܢܐܕܹܡ܃
ܝܹܠ݁ܐܢ ܕ ܠܥܐܕܹܡ܃
ܗܐ ܟܐܢ ܐܲܟ݁ܐ ܐܲܕ ܝܹܢܙ̰ܐܚ.

ܡܐ ܕ ܘ'ܝܠ݁ܐܢ ܕ ܡܹܢܘܐܠܐ܃
ܐܼܨ̰ܘܥܹܢ ܐܼ ܕܹ݁ܘܠܐ܃
ܐܿܪ ܝܹܬ݁ܝܠܝ ܕ ܐܲܠܹܡ݁ܐܡ.
ܡܐ ܠܐ ܝܹܬ݁ܥܐܢܐܕ ܐܿܫܹ݁ܢ܃
ܝܹܣܢܐܥ̰ܐ ܡܹܕܹ݁ܢ܃
ܟܘܠܘܐ ܝܹܣܥ̰ܐܒ‑ܐܣ ܢܐܕܐܡ.

ܠܹܡܩܐܣ݁ܐ ܕܥ̰ܐ ܬܹܓ݁ܘܢܝ‑ܬ܃
ܠܚܝܪܦ̰ܐ‑ܣ ܬܹܣܕܘܠ݁‑ܝܬ܃
ܬ݁ܓܐܡ݁ܝܢ ܡܹܕܹ݁ܢ ܐܲܕ ܬ‑ܘܐܠܝܢ܃
ܝܝܘ݁ܐܣ݁ ܐܿܪ ܢܹܠܗܝ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܐܣ܃
ܐܲܕ ܬ‑ܝܘܹ݁ܬ ܐܿܥܹܣ݁ܐܣ܃
ܐܲܕ ܥ̰ܘܢܦ̰ܘܢ ܘ'ܐܕ ܬ‑ܝܠܐܘܝܢ.

ܬܝܡܹܣ ܐܲܕ ܬܹܟܹ݁ܪ ܕܹܓ ܘܘܠ‑ܝܣ܃
ܐܲܡܙܘܢ ܕܐܝ ܕ ܝܹܒܠܝܣ܃
ܐܿܪ ܝܹܠ݁ܝ ܘ'ܐܕ ܬ݁‑ܝܹܣܹ݁ܚ̰ܣܝܢ.
ܐܲܕ ܕ‑ܝܐܦ̰ ܐܼܡܐܢ‑ܝܣ ܕܝ ܠܟܐܦ̰܃
ܝܹܡܹ݁ܬ ܣ ܢ݁ܫܐܦ̰:
ܕ ܠܚ̰ܹܛ݁ ܢ ܠܹ݁ܗ ܠܚܐܢܝܢ.

ܕ ܣܝ ܪܐܒܹܚ܃ ܐܲܕ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܐܣ ܢܹܢܕܹܡ
ܐܼܡܝ ܕ ܠܦ̰ܐܗܹܡ:
ܬܝܟܠܝ ܐܼܢܹܣ ܬܹܙܓܐ ܬܹܨܦ̰ܐ.
ܝܹܣ݁ܐܟܐܝ ܘܝܕܹܢ ܐܼܥ̰ܹܦ̰ܠܹܢ܃
ܬ݁ܐܦ̰ܹܢ‑ܬ ܝܹܚܒܝܒܹܢ܃
ܣ݁ܘܩ ܝܝܕ‑ܣ ܚܐܫܐ ܠܦ̰ܐܝܕܐ.

ܐܲܟ݁ܐ ܐܲܝ ܕ ܒܘܢܐܕܹܡ ܝܹܠܗܐܢ܃
ܐܼܨ̰ܹܦ̰ܪܹܢ ܐܼܒܹܪܕܐܢ
ܥ̰ܹܦ̰ ܕ‑ܬܘܹܨ݁ܐ ܫ݁ܐܪܝܥܐ.
ܥ̰ܐܣ ܦ̰ܹܠ݁‑ܐܣ ܬܹܘܥܹܪ܃ ܕ݁ܘܢܝܬ܃
ܠܐܡܹܥܢܐ܃ ܐܲܡ ܬܐܪܓܝܬ܃
ܠܚ̰ܐܬ݁ܝܡܐ ܐܼܢܹܣ ܕ ܪܹ݁ܚܡܐ.

Translation.Title: The Conclusion
Paragraphs:
To all those who have listened to me,
You who are not unmindful or simple‑minded,
Reflect deeply upon this tale.
It is for all of you that I have labored,
In order to spare you
God's blows.

Whosoever stands in a position of authority
Let him act with complete uprightness,
So that he may remain mounted, and never be brought low.
Let him give due honor to the great,
And shelter the small,
So that no hand shall ever be lifted against him.

Even the lion, as is well known,
Who was strong enough for any strife,
Was stretched out dead upon the ground.
How much more so for the child of Adam,
Who is made of mere frailty,
In one suspended instant, he plummets into misery.

As for the one who is an ordinary man,
Who obeys the authority of the land,
Let him never become a deceitful plotters.
If he goes about imitating the wolf,
Setting people against one another,
He will steal the sleep from everyone's eyes.

The ultimate retribution is waiting for him,
His treacherous trade will bring him low,
And people will refuse to even look upon him.
One day, an evil day will fall upon him,
The Guardian will strike him down,
And both men and women will turn from him in disgust.

A burning fire will kindle within his heart,
As if he were the Devil himself,
And there will be no one to extinguish it.
He will find himself trapped in a deep chasm,
Dying a parched, agonizing death:
By the strict decree of God the Merciful.

It is for Sir Rabeḥ that we shall grieve,
For he was a man of deep understanding:
His path was ever pure and unblemished.
He awakened those who were heedless,
His friends always found him true,
And dealing with him brought nothing but blessing.

Such is the upright child of Adam,
Who follows the true paths
Decreed by the sacred law.
Though the world may be harsh and unyielding to him,
It passes away just like a dream,
And his ultimate end is mercy.

Translation.Title: Ω
Paragraphs: '''Dive into the heart of Kabyle oral memory through the tricks and adventures of a timeless hero: the wolf.'''

From 1920 to 1942, for over twenty years, Brahim Zellal traveled across Kabylia to gather and preserve this precious cycle of animal fables rooted in popular tradition. First published in 1964, ''The Tale of the Wolf (Le Roman du ''''chacal'''')'' offers a fascinating mirror of society and human relationships, where the wit and cunning of the weak stand up to the strength of the powerful.
A landmark of Amazigh literary heritage, saved from oblivion through a patient and passionate work of collection.

''Translator's Note: Although French editions have traditionally rendered the Kabyle term "Uccen" as "chacal" (jackal), the translator has deliberately chosen "wolf" to remain faithful to the living language and cultural perception of native Kabyle speakers, for whom "Uccen" is the wolf—a linguistic intuition now confirmed by modern genetic studies.''

'''About the Author'''
'''Brahim ''''''Zellal''' (1898–1972) was a high school Arabic teacher in Blida. Holding a bachelor's degree in Arabic and an advanced diploma in Berber studies, he dedicated his dual academic background to the preservation and transmission of Kabyle oral literature.
'''Last revised''' on 2026‑11‑27.
